promises.quote: when you choose a number more than 1, \(we suggest 1, 3 or 5\), the data will be stored on multiple nodes in your cluster using the RAFT protocol as above.
promises.plain: A stream with replicas > 1 keeps each acknowledged message on several nodes, so losing one node does not lose acknowledged data.
promises.when_to_inject: SIGKILL the stream leader while publishes are in flight, right after some publish acks are received
promises.outside_observation: Every publish that got a PubAck (stream seq recorded in Fuss's own log) is still readable at the same sequence with the same payload from the new leader; per-sequence order matches the ack order.
promises.workload_sketch: nats stream add ORDERS --subjects 'orders.>' --replicas 3 --storage file --defaults; loop: nats pub orders.N <uuid> with JetStream acks, logging seq+payload; kill -9 leader (found via nats stream info ORDERS --json); keep publishing; then nats stream get ORDERS <seq> for every logged seq
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: if acks go out before a quorum has durably fsynced (sync interval defaults), a near-simultaneous kill of the leader and one follower could lose acked writes.

promises.quote: The `current` indicates that followers are up to date and have all the messages, here both cluster peers were seen very recently.
promises.plain: A replica reported as 'current' really holds all messages the leader has.
promises.when_to_inject: Stop a follower, publish a batch, restart it, then poll stream info until it reports current
promises.outside_observation: Once nats stream info reports the replica as current, step leadership onto that replica (or kill the others) and verify that its message count, last seq and every logged message match what was acked.
promises.workload_sketch: stream R3; kill follower n3; publish 1000 msgs logging acks; restart n3; poll nats stream info ORDERS --json until n3 current=true; kill the leader and the other follower is not allowed (quorum), so step down repeatedly until n3 is leader; nats stream info and nats stream get each seq
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: 'current' may be judged from lag and heartbeat timing rather than the applied index, so it could flip to current before catch-up has been fully applied or fsynced.

promises.quote: The replica count can be edited once configured.
promises.plain: Changing a stream's replica count keeps all existing messages, and the new replica set ends up holding them.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill one involved node right after issuing nats stream edit --replicas 3 on an R1 stream (or 3->5), while data is being copied
promises.outside_observation: Stream info eventually shows the requested replica count with all replicas current; message count, last seq and contents equal Fuss's ack log, with no gaps or duplicates.
promises.workload_sketch: nats stream add S --replicas 1; publish N msgs logging acks; nats stream edit S --replicas 3 -f; kill -9 a newly chosen peer; restart it; poll nats stream info S --json; verify every seq
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the snapshot or catch-up to new peers may be interrupted by the kill and leave a peer reported current with a partial copy.

promises.quote: Leader elections will represent short interruptions to the stream so if you know you will work on a node later it might be worth moving leadership away from it ahead of time.
promises.plain: A leader election only briefly interrupts the stream; it does not lose or reorder acknowledged messages.
promises.when_to_inject: Issue nats stream cluster step-down repeatedly while several clients publish concurrently, with Nats-Msg-Id set and retries on timeout
promises.outside_observation: The publish error or timeout window is bounded (seconds). All acked messages are present and the per-subject order matches the ack seq order. Retries with the same Nats-Msg-Id inside the duplicate window do not create duplicates.
promises.workload_sketch: R3 stream with duplicate_window 2m; 4 publishers using msg-id headers, retrying on timeout; every 2s run nats stream cluster step-down ORDERS; afterwards read the whole stream and compare against the ack log, checking for duplicate msg-ids
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the dedupe state may not carry over to the new leader, so a retry after a timed-out publish could be stored twice.

promises.quote: Moving leadership away from a node does not remove it from the cluster and does not prevent it from becoming a leader again, this is merely a triggered leader election.
promises.plain: After a step-down, the old leader stays a replica and can become leader again.
promises.when_to_inject: Right after a step-down, then later step down repeatedly or kill the other replicas' leadership
promises.outside_observation: nats stream info still lists the old leader as a replica (current), and after further step-downs it shows up as leader again at some point.
promises.workload_sketch: nats stream cluster step-down ORDERS; record old leader; check nats stream info lists it as a replica; loop step-down up to 10 times until it is leader again
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a node that just stepped down could be held in a backoff state and repeatedly skipped, or its consumer groups might not rejoin.

promises.quote: The same is true for consumers, `nats consumer cluster step-down ORDERS NEW`.
promises.plain: Stepping down a consumer leader is just an election; the consumer keeps its delivery and ack state.
promises.when_to_inject: During active pull and ack traffic on a durable R3 consumer, issue consumer step-down
promises.outside_observation: No acked message is redelivered beyond the at-least-once allowance (it is not redelivered after its ack was confirmed via AckSync). No message is skipped. The consumer's ack floor never moves backwards across elections.
promises.workload_sketch: nats consumer add ORDERS NEW --pull --ack explicit; consumer loop: fetch, AckSync, log seq; every 2s nats consumer cluster step-down ORDERS NEW; check that the union of logged seqs covers 1..N, and list redeliveries of already-acked seqs
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: acks that are in flight during the election could be dropped, and the ack floor reverting would cause redelivery of confirmed acks.

promises.quote: Similar to Streams and Consumers above the Meta Group allows leader stand down.
promises.plain: Stepping down the meta leader elects a new meta leader without losing stream or consumer definitions.
promises.when_to_inject: Issue nats server cluster step-down while concurrently creating and deleting streams
promises.outside_observation: A new meta leader is reported. Every stream create that returned success exists afterwards with its config, and every successful delete stays deleted.
promises.workload_sketch: loop creating streams T1..Tn and deleting some, logging the API results; run nats server cluster step-down --user admin repeatedly; afterwards nats stream ls and compare against the log
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a create proposal acked by the old leader but not yet committed may vanish or reappear after the election.

promises.quote: Generally when shutting down NATS, including using Lame Duck Mode, the cluster will notice this and continue to function.
promises.plain: When a single node shuts down or crashes, the cluster keeps serving JetStream.
promises.when_to_inject: SIGKILL (and separately lame-duck via nats-server --signal ldm) one node of five during steady publish/consume
promises.outside_observation: Publishes to R3 streams keep getting acks after a bounded pause. The meta report marks the node offline / not current. No acked data is lost.
promises.workload_sketch: 5-node cluster; R3 streams with publishers and consumers running; kill -9 n2; watch publish ack latency and nats server report jetstream (Offline=true for n2); verify the ack log against stream contents
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: if the killed node held meta, stream and consumer leadership at once, overlapping elections could stall the API longer than expected.

promises.quote: In the Meta Group report the server `n2-c1` is not current and has not been seen for 9 seconds, it's also behind by 2 raft operations.
promises.plain: The meta group report shows a dead or lagging node as not current or offline, with its lag and last-seen time.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill one node, then do meta operations (create streams) so that it falls behind
promises.outside_observation: /jsz or nats server req jetstream --leader shows that peer with current=false, an offline flag, active growing and lag > 0. After restart it returns to current with lag 0.
promises.workload_sketch: kill -9 n3; nats stream add X1..X3; nats server req jetstream --leader --user admin; check the meta peer fields; restart n3; poll until current
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the offline detection timeout could make the report claim the peer is current for a while after it died.

promises.quote: After the node is removed the cluster will notice that the replica count of a stream is not honored anymore and will immediately pick a new node and start replicating data to it. The new node will be selected using the same placement rules as the existing stream.
promises.plain: After a peer-remove, the stream gets a new replica within its placement rules and copies all data to it, restoring the replica count.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill node n4 permanently, run server-level peer-remove, and keep publishing while the new replica catches up
promises.outside_observation: Stream info shows the replica count back at 3 with a new peer that satisfies the placement tags/cluster. The new peer eventually reports current, and its data matches the ack log (verify by making it leader).
promises.workload_sketch: R3 stream with placement tags; kill -9 n4; nats server cluster peer-remove n4-c1 -f --user admin; keep publishing; poll nats stream info ORDERS --json; once current, step down until the new peer leads and verify all seqs
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: replication to the new peer may race with ongoing publishes and miss messages written between the snapshot and the start of streaming.

promises.quote: At this point the stream and all consumers will have removed `n4-c1` from the group. A new node will be selected, and data will be replicated to it.
promises.plain: A stream-level peer-remove takes the node out of the stream and all of its consumers, replaces it, and keeps the consumers' state intact.
promises.when_to_inject: Run nats stream cluster peer-remove while consumers are actively fetching and acking
promises.outside_observation: Stream and consumer info no longer list n4. The consumer replica sets are restored. Acked messages are not lost from the stream, and consumer progress does not regress.
promises.workload_sketch: R3 stream with 2 durable R3 consumers doing fetch/AckSync; nats stream cluster peer-remove ORDERS n4-c1; nats consumer info for each consumer, checking cluster peers; compare consumer delivered/ack floor with Fuss's log
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a consumer group could keep n4 or lose its leader's ack state if the consumer leader was on n4.

promises.quote: It can be performed with nodes that are still online, but in this case, JetStream will be disabled on those nodes.
promises.plain: Peer-removing an online server disables JetStream on that server.
promises.when_to_inject: Peer-remove a node that is still running
promises.outside_observation: That server's /jsz (or nats server req jetstream --name) reports JetStream disabled, and JetStream API calls routed only to it fail or are not served by it.
promises.workload_sketch: nats server cluster peer-remove n5-c1 -f --user admin while n5 is up; curl n5:8222/jsz; nats server report jetstream
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the disable may not stick if the node restarts or reconnects, and it could rejoin as a JetStream peer.

promises.quote: In order to ensure data consistency across complete restarts, a quorum of servers is required. A quorum is ½ cluster size + 1. This is the minimum number of nodes to ensure at least one node has the most recent data and state after a catastrophic failure.
promises.plain: Every message the cluster acknowledged was stored by a quorum, so after all servers crash and restart, the stream still contains every acknowledged message with its original sequence number.
promises.when_to_inject: SIGKILL all three nats-server processes at once while publishes are in flight, then restart them all.
promises.outside_observation: Compare Fuss's log of PubAck (stream, seq) pairs with a full read of the stream after restart. Every acked seq must be present with the same payload. No acked seq may be missing or changed.
promises.workload_sketch: nats stream add S --replicas 3 --subjects s.>; loop: js.Publish(s.x, unique payload), log ack seq; kill -9 all three servers; restart all three; wait for the stream leader; nats stream get S <seq> or an ordered consumer reading from seq 1; diff against the log.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the RAFT log or message block may be acked after quorum replication but before an fsync on the followers, so a simultaneous kill could lose the tail.

promises.quote: So for a cluster size of 3, you’ll need at least two JetStream enabled NATS servers available to store new messages. For a cluster size of 5, you’ll need at least 3 NATS servers, and so forth.
promises.plain: With a majority of servers up, new messages are stored and acknowledged. Below a majority, no new message is acknowledged.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill one of three servers and check that writes continue. Then kill a second server and check that writes stop.
promises.outside_observation: With 2 of 3 up, PubAcks arrive. With 1 of 3 up, publishes time out or return errors and no PubAck arrives. After the majority is restored, no message published during the minority period shows up as if it had been acked.
promises.workload_sketch: R3 stream; continuous js.Publish with a short timeout; kill -9 n3 and record ack success; kill -9 n2 and record ack failures; restart n2 and n3; read the stream and check it contains only acked seqs plus possibly unacked-but-stored ones, with no gaps in acked seqs.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a lone surviving former leader might briefly ack writes before it notices it lost quorum.

promises.quote: The elected leader handles ACKs and so forth, if there is no leader the stream will not accept messages.
promises.plain: A stream with no elected leader never acknowledges a publish.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill the current stream leader, found with nats stream info, during a steady stream of publishes.
promises.outside_observation: During the election gap, publishes get no ack or get an error. After a new leader is elected, the acked sequence numbers keep increasing with no duplicate seqs. Every seq acked before the kill is still readable.
promises.workload_sketch: R3 stream; publisher loop logging acks and errors with timestamps; nats stream info S to find the leader; kill -9 the leader; keep publishing; restart the killed server; verify all acked seqs exist and are unique.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the old leader might ack a message just before dying that the new leader never received, which would leave an acked message missing.

promises.quote: Stream Group - each Stream creates a RAFT group, this group synchronizes state and data between its members.
promises.plain: All replicas of a stream hold the same messages in the same order, so after leader changes the stream's contents and sequence order stay consistent.
promises.when_to_inject: Repeatedly kill and restart different servers, each time forcing a leader change, while publishing.
promises.outside_observation: After things settle, step the leader to each server in turn with nats stream cluster step-down and read the whole stream each time. Every read must match exactly: same seqs, same payloads, same order. The message count and last seq from nats stream info must agree.
promises.workload_sketch: R3 stream; publisher loop; a chaos loop that kills -9 a random server and restarts it after N seconds; at the end, for each server: step down until that server is leader, then dump the stream; compare the dumps against each other and against the ack log.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a follower that restarts during a snapshot catch-up might keep a divergent tail that only shows up once it becomes leader.

promises.quote: Consumer Group - each Consumer creates a RAFT group, this group synchronizes consumer state between its members. The group will live on the machines where the Stream Group is and handle consumption ACKs etc.
promises.plain: Consumer ack state is replicated, so after the consumer leader crashes, messages that were already acked are not delivered again as unacked and the delivery position is not lost.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill the consumer leader, found with nats consumer info, right after a batch of acks has been confirmed with AckSync.
promises.outside_observation: Fuss logs each stream seq whose AckSync succeeded. After failover, no AckSync-confirmed seq is redelivered. The ack floor in nats consumer info is at or above the highest contiguous confirmed seq.
promises.workload_sketch: R3 stream with N messages; durable pull consumer with explicit ack; fetch and AckSync in a loop, logging seqs; kill -9 the consumer leader; continue fetching; restart the server; check for redelivered seqs that had a confirmed ack.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the ack reply might go out after the leader applies it locally but before it is replicated to the other consumer replicas.

promises.quote: Meta Group - all servers join the Meta Group and the JetStream API is managed by this group. A leader is elected and this owns the API and takes care of server placement.
promises.plain: If the meta leader dies, a new one is elected and JetStream API calls such as stream create work again, without losing or duplicating stream and consumer definitions.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill the meta leader, found with nats server report jetstream, while API calls like stream add and consumer add are in flight.
promises.outside_observation: Every stream or consumer whose create call returned success still exists after failover and restart. Calls that failed either did not create anything or created exactly one object. Stream ls shows no duplicates and no missing objects.
promises.workload_sketch: Loop: nats stream add S_i --replicas 3, logging success or failure; kill -9 the meta leader mid-loop; continue; restart it; nats stream ls; diff against the log.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a create acknowledged by the old meta leader might not be committed in the meta RAFT log before the crash.

promises.quote: For example, if 5 servers are JetStream enabled you would want two servers in one “zone”, two servers in another, and the remaining server in a third. This means you can lose any one “zone” at any time and continue operating.
promises.plain: In a 5-node cluster, losing any two servers that form a zone still lets publishes be acked and consumers work.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill two servers at the same moment during a publish and consume workload.
promises.outside_observation: Publishes resume getting acks after re-election. Consumers keep receiving messages. No acked message is lost after the killed servers restart.
promises.workload_sketch: 5-node cluster; R3 and R5 streams; publish and consume loops; kill -9 n1 and n2 together; observe; restart both; verify the ack log against the stream contents.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: R3 streams whose peers sit on 2 of the killed nodes lose quorum, because placement does not know about zones unless tags are configured. So 'continue operating' may hold only for R5, or with zone tags.

promises.quote: After two servers are running you'll be ready to use JetStream.
promises.plain: With only two of the three configured servers started, JetStream is usable and accepts R3 stream creation and publishes.
promises.when_to_inject: Cold start the cluster with only n1 and n2. Start n3 later.
promises.outside_observation: Stream add and publish succeed with two nodes. When n3 joins, it catches up, and reading the stream with n3 as leader shows all previously acked messages.
promises.workload_sketch: Start n1 and n2 with empty store dirs; nats stream add S --replicas 3; publish N messages and log acks; start n3; step down until n3 is leader; read the stream and compare.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: R3 stream placement may refuse to create the stream when only 2 peers are known, contradicting the 'ready' claim for replicated streams.

promises.quote: Unlike [Core NATS](https://docs.nats.io/nats-concepts/core-nats), which provides an at most once delivery guarantee, a consumer in JetStream can provide an at least **once delivery** guarantee.
promises.plain: Every message stored in the stream is delivered to a consumer at least once.
promises.when_to_inject: SIGKILL nats-server while a durable AckExplicit pull consumer is mid-batch: some messages are delivered but not yet acked, some acks are in flight, and new publishes are still arriving.
promises.outside_observation: Fuss logs every publish that got a positive PubAck (stream seq) and every delivered message (stream seq, delivery count) to its own history file. After restart and drain, every PubAck'd seq must appear in the deliveries at least once.
promises.workload_sketch: nats stream add S --subjects 's.>' --storage file; nats consumer add S C --pull --ack explicit --deliver all; loop: nats pub s.x <n> (record PubAck seq); in parallel loop: nats consumer next S C --count 10 --ack; kill -9 server; restart server; keep running nats consumer next until no messages arrive for 2x AckWait.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the consumer's stored ack floor could be flushed ahead of the actual acks, or a PubAck could be sent before the message is synced, so a message is silently skipped after a crash.

promises.quote: This tracking ensures that if a message is not acknowledged (un-acked or 'nacked'), the consumer will automatically attempt to re-deliver it.
promises.plain: A message that is delivered but not acked, or that is nacked, gets delivered again.
promises.when_to_inject: Pull messages without acking (or send -NAK), then restart the server before redelivery happens.
promises.outside_observation: After restart, each un-acked or nacked seq is delivered again with a higher delivery count (from the message metadata), and is not dropped.
promises.workload_sketch: nats consumer add S C --pull --ack explicit --wait 5s; nats pub s.x 1..20; nats consumer next S C --count 20 --no-ack; nak half of them via a client; kill -9 server; restart; nats consumer next S C --count 20 --ack; compare seqs.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: pending/redelivery state lives in memory and is written lazily, so it could be lost on a crash.

promises.quote: If a message is not acknowledged within a user-specified number of delivery attempts, an advisory notification is emitted.
promises.plain: When a message hits MaxDeliver without being acked, the server publishes a max-deliveries advisory.
promises.when_to_inject: Restart the server after a message has used up some, but not all, of its MaxDeliver attempts.
promises.outside_observation: A subscriber on $JS.EVENT.ADVISORY.CONSUMER.MAX_DELIVERIES.S.C gets exactly one advisory for that stream seq, sent after the MaxDeliver-th delivery, not earlier and not never.
promises.workload_sketch: nats sub '$JS.EVENT.ADVISORY.CONSUMER.MAX_DELIVERIES.>' (logged); nats consumer add S C --pull --ack explicit --max-deliver 4 --wait 2s; nats pub s.x m; nats consumer next S C --no-ack twice; kill -9; restart; nats consumer next S C --no-ack until no more deliveries; count deliveries and advisories.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the delivery count could reset or roll back after restart, giving extra deliveries, or the advisory could be emitted only by the in-memory path and be lost around the restart.

promises.quote: No acknowledgements (if gap is detected, consumer is recreated)
promises.plain: An ordered consumer gives the client stream messages in order with no gaps. On a gap, it recreates itself and resumes.
promises.when_to_inject: Restart or kill the server while an ordered consumer is streaming a large backlog.
promises.outside_observation: The sequence of stream seqs the client receives strictly increases and has no holes (ignoring seqs deleted from the stream). Duplicates appear only where the client recreated the consumer.
promises.workload_sketch: publish 100k messages to S; run a Go client with js.OrderedConsumer / nats sub --stream S (ordered) and log stream seqs; kill -9 server mid-read; restart; let the client finish; check that seqs are monotonic and gap-free.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the client's gap detection works from consumer seq, and a reconnect could resume from the wrong stream seq after the server-side ephemeral is lost.

promises.quote: If set, clients can have subscriptions bind to the consumer and _resume_ until the consumer is explicitly deleted.
promises.plain: A durable consumer survives server restarts and clients can resume it from where it left off.
promises.when_to_inject: SIGKILL the server repeatedly while clients consume and ack from a durable consumer.
promises.outside_observation: After each restart, nats consumer info S C still shows the consumer. Delivery resumes from just past the last acked seq that Fuss recorded, not from the start and not skipping ahead.
promises.workload_sketch: nats consumer add S D --pull --ack explicit; consume and ack 1000 msgs, logging acks; kill -9; restart; nats consumer info S D; nats consumer next S D --count 10; compare the first seq with Fuss's last confirmed ack.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the consumer's metadata or state file could be partly written during a crash, so on restart the consumer is missing or reset.

promises.quote: By default, consumers will have the same replication factor as the stream they consume, and will remain even when there are periods of inactivity (unless `InactiveThreshold` is set explicitly). Consumers can recover from server and client failure.
promises.plain: Durable consumers without InactiveThreshold persist through idle periods and through server or client crashes.
promises.when_to_inject: Leave the consumer idle with no bound clients, kill the server, and keep it down for a long time (or move the clock forward) before restarting.
promises.outside_observation: nats consumer ls S still lists the consumer, and its ack floor (nats consumer info) matches Fuss's recorded acks.
promises.workload_sketch: nats consumer add S D --pull; ack some msgs; disconnect all clients; kill -9; advance the system clock by days; restart; nats consumer info S D.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: inactivity timing could compare against wall-clock timestamps from before the restart and wrongly treat the consumer as expired.

promises.quote: Durables and ephemeral have the same message delivery semantics but an ephemeral consumer will not have persisted state or fault tolerance (server memory only) and will be automatically _cleaned up_ (deleted) after a period of inactivity, when no subscriptions are bound to the consumer.
promises.plain: An ephemeral consumer is deleted only after InactiveThreshold of inactivity with no bound subscriptions, not before.
promises.when_to_inject: While an ephemeral consumer has an active subscription, or has been idle for less than its InactiveThreshold, jump the server host clock forward or backward.
promises.outside_observation: The consumer stays (nats consumer info) while a subscription is bound or the idle time measured by Fuss's monotonic clock is under the threshold. It disappears soon after the threshold once nothing is bound.
promises.workload_sketch: create an ephemeral pull consumer with --inactive-threshold 30s from a client; keep pulling every 5s; jump the clock +1h; check it still exists; stop pulling; check it is gone about 30s later by monotonic time.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the inactivity check could use wall-clock time, so a forward jump deletes an active consumer and a backward jump keeps a dead one forever.

promises.quote: The duration that the server will wait for an acknowledgment for any individual message _once it has been delivered to a consumer_. If an acknowledgment is not received in time, the message will be redelivered.
promises.plain: An un-acked message is redelivered about AckWait after delivery, not much sooner and not much later.
promises.when_to_inject: Right after a message is delivered without an ack, step the server clock forward or backward by much more than AckWait.
promises.outside_observation: Fuss's monotonic clock shows the gap between first delivery and redelivery is close to AckWait. A large clock step should not cause instant redelivery or a stalled redelivery.
promises.workload_sketch: nats consumer add S C --pull --ack explicit --wait 10s; nats pub s.x m; nats consumer next S C --no-ack (record t0); date -s '+1 hour' on the server host; poll nats consumer next S C and record t1; repeat with -1 hour.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: redelivery deadlines could be stored as wall-clock timestamps, so a backward step delays redelivery by the size of the step.

promises.quote: Once this limit is reached, message delivery will be suspended. This limit applies across _all_ of the consumer's bound subscriptions.
promises.plain: Across all clients of a consumer, there are never more than MaxAckPending un-acked messages outstanding.
promises.when_to_inject: Many clients pull or receive pushes at the same time without acking, plus a server restart while the limit is reached.
promises.outside_observation: From Fuss's log, the number of distinct seqs delivered and not yet acked or expired never exceeds MaxAckPending at any time, including just after restart. nats consumer info Num Ack Pending stays at or below the limit.
promises.workload_sketch: nats consumer add S C --pull --ack explicit --max-pending 50 --wait 60s; publish 1000; run 10 concurrent clients doing nats consumer next --count 20 --no-ack; kill -9; restart; repeat the pulls; count outstanding.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: after restart the pending set might not be rebuilt before delivery resumes, letting another full window go out on top of the old one.

promises.quote: The maximum number of times a specific message delivery will be attempted. Applies to any message that is re-sent due to acknowledgment policy (i.e., due to a negative acknowledgment or no acknowledgment sent by the client). The default is -1 (redeliver until acknowledged). Messages that have reached the maximum delivery count will stay in the stream.
promises.plain: No message is delivered more than MaxDeliver times, even across restarts, and it stays in the stream after the limit is reached.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill the server between delivery attempts of a message that keeps being nacked.
promises.outside_observation: Fuss's count of deliveries per seq (and the server's delivery count in metadata) never goes above MaxDeliver. After the limit, nats stream get S <seq> still returns the message.
promises.workload_sketch: nats consumer add S C --pull --ack explicit --max-deliver 3; nats pub s.x m; loop: nats consumer next S C and send -NAK; kill -9 after the 2nd delivery; restart; continue the loop for a while; nats stream get S 1.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the delivery count is updated in memory before it is persisted, so a crash could roll it back and allow extra deliveries.

promises.quote: When `MaxDeliver` is larger than the backoff list, the last delay in the list will apply for the remaining deliveries. Note that backoff is NOT applied to `nak`ed messages. A `nak` will result in immediate re-delivery unless `nakWithDelay` is used to set the re-delivery delay explicitly. When `BackOff` is set, it **overrides `AckWait` entirely**. The first value in the BackOff determines the `AckWait` value.
promises.plain: Ack-timeout redeliveries follow the BackOff schedule (the last value repeats). A nak redelivers immediately, or after the nak delay if one is given.
promises.when_to_inject: Restart the server partway through a backoff schedule, and also step the clock during a long backoff delay.
promises.outside_observation: Gaps between redeliveries measured by Fuss's monotonic clock match the schedule (first = BackOff[0], later ones = BackOff[i], tail = last value). Nak'd messages come back right away, or after the given delay.
promises.workload_sketch: nats consumer add S C --pull --ack explicit --max-deliver 6 --backoff-steps or a client with BackOff=[2s,5s,10s]; publish m; pull with no ack and record each redelivery time; kill -9 after the 2nd; restart; continue. Separately: pull, NakWithDelay(7s), record.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: after restart the delivery count or the next-due time is rebuilt wrongly, so the schedule restarts at BackOff[0] or fires everything at once.

promises.quote: `AckAll`: Acknowledge only the last message received in a series; all previous messages are automatically acknowledged. Will acknowledge all pending messages for all subscribers for Pull Consumer.
promises.plain: With AckAll, acking seq N also acks every earlier pending message, for all subscribers, and this holds after a crash.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill the server right after the server confirms an AckAll for seq N (double-ack / AckSync returns).
promises.outside_observation: After restart, no seq at or below N is redelivered to any subscriber, and the ack floor in nats consumer info is at least N.
promises.workload_sketch: nats consumer add S C --pull --ack all; publish 100; two clients pull 50 each; client B AckSync on the highest seq; kill -9 immediately; restart; pull until empty and check that no seq <= N comes back.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the confirmed ack could be replied to before the floor is stored durably, so a crash brings earlier messages back.

promises.quote: `AckNone`: No acknowledgment needed; the server assumes acknowledgment on delivery.
promises.plain: With AckNone, a delivered message is treated as acked and is not redelivered.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill the server while it is pushing or pulling messages to an AckNone durable consumer.
promises.outside_observation: After restart, Fuss records how many already-delivered seqs come back. Any duplicate counts against the promise, but a small replay window right after a crash should be reported separately as a possible flush lag.
promises.workload_sketch: nats consumer add S C --pull --ack none; publish 10k; pull continuously and log seqs; kill -9; restart; pull until empty; find duplicates.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the delivered pointer is persisted lazily, so the server rolls back to an older position and resends messages.

promises.quote: > **Warning**: The server may consider an acknowledgment arriving out of the window. For instance, in a queue situation, if a first process fails to acknowledge within the window and the message has been redelivered to another consumer, the acknowledgment from the first consumer will be considered.
promises.plain: A late ack from the first receiver still counts after the message has been redelivered to someone else.
promises.when_to_inject: Client A acks after AckWait has expired and the message has already gone to client B, which never acks.
promises.outside_observation: The message is not redelivered again after A's late ack. nats consumer info shows it acked (ack floor moves past it).
promises.workload_sketch: nats consumer add S C --pull --ack explicit --wait 3s; publish m; client A pulls and sleeps 5s; client B pulls (gets the redelivery) and does not ack; A acks with AckSync; wait 10s and check that no more deliveries occur.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the server could ignore the ack because it refers to an older delivery count.

promises.quote: `DeliverByStartTime`: Start with messages on or after the specified time. The consumer must specify `OptStartTime` defining the start time.
promises.plain: A start-time consumer delivers exactly the messages whose stored timestamp is on or after OptStartTime.
promises.when_to_inject: Step the server clock backward while messages are being published, then create the consumer.
promises.outside_observation: Compare the delivered seqs with the timestamps from nats stream get. Every delivered message has a timestamp >= OptStartTime, and no stored message with timestamp >= OptStartTime is missing. Report any non-monotonic timestamps caused by the skew.
promises.workload_sketch: publish batch A; date -s '-10 min'; publish batch B; date -s '+20 min'; publish batch C; nats consumer add S T --pull --deliver <time> ; pull all; check against nats stream get timestamps.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the server may find the start position by binary search on timestamps it assumes are monotonic, so skewed timestamps cause skips.

promises.quote: `DeliverNew`: Start receiving messages created after the consumer was created.
promises.plain: A DeliverNew durable delivers every message published after its creation and none from before, also after a restart.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill the server shortly after the consumer is created but before it has delivered anything.
promises.outside_observation: After restart, delivered seqs are exactly the PubAck'd seqs published after the consumer-create response. No earlier seqs appear and no later ones are missing.
promises.workload_sketch: publish 100; nats consumer add S N --pull --deliver new (record time and last seq); publish 100; kill -9; restart; publish 100; pull until empty.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: if the start position is not persisted at creation, it could be recomputed on restart as 'new as of now' and skip the messages in between.

promises.quote: If the policy is `ReplayOriginal`, the messages in the stream will be pushed to the client at the same rate they were originally received, simulating the original timing.
promises.plain: ReplayOriginal reproduces the gaps between messages as they were originally published.
promises.when_to_inject: Step the server clock during replay, or publish with a clock step in the middle.
promises.outside_observation: Gaps between deliveries, measured on Fuss's monotonic clock, should match the gaps between stored timestamps. Report any huge stall or burst caused by the clock step.
promises.workload_sketch: publish 20 msgs with 1s spacing; nats consumer add S R --deliver all --replay original --target r.out; nats sub r.out and record arrival times; step the server clock -1h midway.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: pacing might compute wall-clock deadlines, so a backward step pauses replay for an hour.

promises.quote: The queue group name used to distribute messages among subscribers. Analogous to a [queue group](https://docs.nats.io/nats-concepts/core-nats/queue) in core NATS.
promises.plain: Each delivery of a push consumer with a DeliverGroup goes to only one member of the group.
promises.when_to_inject: Several queue subscribers are bound while some disconnect and reconnect and the server restarts.
promises.outside_observation: For each (seq, delivery count) pair, only one subscriber logs receipt. Duplicates only appear as redeliveries with a higher delivery count.
promises.workload_sketch: nats consumer add S Q --target q.out --deliver-group g --ack explicit; start 5 nats sub q.out --queue g that log and ack; publish 10k; kill -9 and restart the server mid-run; compare logs.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: during reconnect the server could briefly treat members as separate interest and send the same delivery to two of them.

promises.quote: If set, forces the consumer state to be kept in memory rather than inherit the storage type of the stream (default is file storage).
promises.plain: With MemoryStorage set, the consumer's state is not written into the file store.
promises.when_to_inject: During consumption and acks on a file-backed stream with a memory-storage consumer, then restart.
promises.outside_observation: Read-only inspection of the JetStream store dir shows no ack state for this consumer under the stream's obs/ directory. Compare with a sibling file-backed durable to confirm Fuss is looking in the right place.
promises.workload_sketch: nats stream add S --storage file; create consumer M with MemoryStorage=true via a client and file-backed durable F; consume and ack on both; ls -R <store>/jetstream/<acct>/streams/S/obs; kill -9; restart; nats consumer info for M and F.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the on-disk layout is undocumented, so Fuss may misread the store. Also the server could still write metadata or snapshots for memory consumers.

promises.quote: Defines the maximum number of messages, without acknowledgment, that can be outstanding. Once this limit is reached, message delivery will be suspended.
promises.plain: When the disk fills while acks are flowing, outstanding deliveries still never exceed MaxAckPending, and acked messages are not later redelivered as if they were never acked.
promises.when_to_inject: Fill the filesystem holding the JetStream store while clients are acking a durable consumer at a high rate.
promises.outside_observation: Fuss records which acks were confirmed (AckSync success) and which errored. After freeing space and restarting, confirmed acks are never redelivered, unconfirmed ones may be, and outstanding never exceeds MaxAckPending.
promises.workload_sketch: store on a small loopback filesystem; nats consumer add S C --pull --ack explicit --max-pending 100; publish to near capacity; fallocate filler to fill the disk; consume with AckSync and log the results; remove filler; kill -9; restart; drain.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a failed write of consumer state might be swallowed while the AckSync reply still reports success.

promises.quote: JetStream support idempotent message writes by ignoring duplicate messages as indicated by the `Nats-Msg-Id` header.
promises.plain: Publishing the same Nats-Msg-Id more than once within the window stores the message only once, even across a server crash and restart.
promises.when_to_inject: Right after the server acks the first publish with a given Msg-Id. Repeat with the kill landing while that first publish is still in flight with no ack yet.
promises.outside_observation: After restart, retry the publish with the same Msg-Id. Then check stream info message count and the stream messages: exactly one message per Msg-Id. The PubAck on the retry should have duplicate=true when the first copy was stored.
promises.workload_sketch: nats stream add ORDERS --subjects 'ORDERS.*' --dupe-window 2m --storage file; nats req -H Nats-Msg-Id:1 ORDERS.new hello1; kill -9 nats-server; restart; nats req -H Nats-Msg-Id:1 ORDERS.new hello2; nats stream info ORDERS; nats stream get ORDERS 1
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the in-memory dedup table may be rebuilt from disk on restart, and may miss entries whose message was written but not yet synced. That could let a duplicate through.

promises.quote: and in the output you can see that the duplicate publications were detected and only one message (the first one) is actually stored in the stream
promises.plain: When duplicates race, the body that ends up stored is the first one accepted, and later bodies with the same ID are discarded.
promises.when_to_inject: Fire many publishes with the same Msg-Id and different bodies at once from separate connections. Optionally kill the server mid-burst.
promises.outside_observation: Exactly one stored message. Its body matches the one publish whose PubAck had duplicate=false, and every other PubAck reports duplicate=true.
promises.workload_sketch: Start N goroutines, each running js.Publish("ORDERS.new", body_i, nats.MsgId("X")) and recording each PubAck; then nats stream get ORDERS <seq>
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a race between the dedup check and the store append could let two copies in, or make two publishers both see duplicate=false.

promises.quote: The default window to track duplicates in is 2 minutes, this can be set on the command line using `--dupe-window` when creating a stream, though we would caution against large windows.
promises.plain: Duplicates are rejected for the configured window (2 minutes by default) and accepted again once it has passed.
promises.when_to_inject: Between the first publish and a retry with the same Msg-Id: step the host wall clock forward or backward, or restart the server, while the window should still be open.
promises.outside_observation: A retry inside the real elapsed window gets duplicate=true and the message count stays the same. A retry after the window adds a new message.
promises.workload_sketch: nats stream add ORDERS --dupe-window 30s; nats req -H Nats-Msg-Id:a ORDERS.new x; skew clock +5m (or restart); nats req -H Nats-Msg-Id:a ORDERS.new y; nats stream info ORDERS
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: window expiry may use the wall clock instead of a monotonic clock, so a forward skew could expire dedup entries early.

promises.quote: if you send a `Request()` to a subject covered by the configuration of the Stream the service will reply to you once it stored the message.
promises.plain: A positive publish ack means the message is durably stored and will still be there after a crash.
promises.when_to_inject: Immediately after the client receives the PubAck, before any graceful shutdown.
promises.outside_observation: Every message whose PubAck Fuss logged is present at its acked sequence after restart, with the same body. No acked sequence is missing or holds a different body.
promises.workload_sketch: Loop: nats req ORDERS.new msg-$i, logging the sequence from each PubAck; kill -9 at a random moment; restart; nats stream get ORDERS <seq> for every logged sequence
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: file store writes may be buffered and fsync'd lazily (sync interval), so acked data in the OS page cache could be lost if the whole host loses power. A plain process kill is less likely to lose it.

promises.quote: If the response received from the server indicates success you can be sure that the message will never be re-delivered by the consumer (due to a loss of your acknowledgement).
promises.plain: Once an AckSync succeeds, that message is never delivered again by that consumer, even after a server crash.
promises.when_to_inject: Right after the client receives a successful AckSync response.
promises.outside_observation: After restart, keep fetching from the same durable consumer until no messages remain and AckWait has passed. No message that was AckSync'd shows up again.
promises.workload_sketch: nats consumer add ORDERS DISPATCH --pull --ack explicit; client fetches and calls msg.AckSync() for each, logging the stream sequence; kill -9; restart; fetch repeatedly and compare against the log
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: consumer state (ack floor) may be persisted asynchronously from the ack reply, so a crash could roll the ack floor back.

promises.quote: JetStream supports Exactly Once publication and consumption by combining Message Deduplication and double acks.
promises.plain: With Msg-Id dedup on publish and AckSync on consume, each logical message is stored once and processed once end to end.
promises.when_to_inject: At random points while the publisher retries timed-out publishes with the same Msg-Id and the consumer AckSyncs.
promises.outside_observation: Fuss's own log shows each Msg-Id stored once (stream count equals unique IDs). Each Msg-Id has exactly one successful AckSync and no delivery after that successful AckSync.
promises.workload_sketch: Publisher: for id in 1..N, retry js.Publish(..., MsgId(id)) until PubAck. Consumer: fetch, record, AckSync. Kill and restart the server repeatedly, then reconcile the logs.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: retries that straddle a restart plus lazily persisted dedup or ack state could produce a second copy or a redelivery.

promises.quote: In `WorkQueuePolicy` the messages will be removed as soon as _the_ Consumer received an Acknowledgement.
promises.plain: In a work-queue stream, an acked message is removed and never comes back, even after a restart.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill or restart the server right after a successful AckSync on a work-queue stream.
promises.outside_observation: Stream message count drops by one per ack and stays that way after restart. A get on an acked sequence returns not found. The acked message is never redelivered.
promises.workload_sketch: nats stream add Q --retention work --subjects 'q.*'; nats consumer add Q W --pull --ack explicit; publish 100; fetch, AckSync 50; kill -9; restart; nats stream info Q; fetch the rest
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the stream-side delete and the consumer ack floor are persisted separately, so a crash between them could resurrect the message or lose an unacked one.

promises.quote: each subject captured by the stream can only have one consumer at a time
promises.plain: A work-queue stream rejects a second consumer whose filter overlaps an existing one.
promises.when_to_inject: Issue several consumer-create calls with overlapping filters at the same moment, optionally around a restart.
promises.outside_observation: At most one create succeeds. nats consumer ls shows no two consumers with overlapping filters, and this still holds after restart.
promises.workload_sketch: Run in parallel: nats consumer add Q A --pull --filter q.x & nats consumer add Q B --pull --filter 'q.*' & ...; then nats consumer ls Q and inspect each consumer's filter
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the overlap check and the consumer registration might not be atomic under concurrent creates.

promises.quote: Once all currently defined consumers have received explicit acknowledgement from a subscribing application for the message it is then removed from the stream.
promises.plain: In an interest stream, a message stays until every consumer has acked it, then it is removed, and this holds across restart.
promises.when_to_inject: Restart after one consumer has acked and another has not, and again after both have acked.
promises.outside_observation: The message is still present while any consumer has not acked it, including after restart. It is gone once all consumers have acked it.
promises.workload_sketch: nats stream add I --retention interest; add consumers C1 and C2; publish 1; C1 AckSync; kill -9; restart; nats stream info I (expect 1); C2 AckSync; restart; nats stream info I (expect 0)
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: interest tracking may be recomputed on restart from consumer state that lags the acks, causing early removal or a message that never gets removed.

promises.quote: In all Retention Policies the basic limits apply as upper bounds, these are `MaxMsgs` for how many messages are kept in total, `MaxBytes` for how big the set can be in total and `MaxAge` for what is the oldest message that will be kept.
promises.plain: The stream never holds more than MaxMsgs messages or MaxBytes bytes, or messages older than MaxAge.
promises.when_to_inject: Step the wall clock forward or backward while messages are near MaxAge. Separately, kill the server during heavy publishing at the count or byte limit.
promises.outside_observation: Stream info never reports more than the limits after things settle. No message whose original timestamp is older than MaxAge (measured on Fuss's own clock) remains. Under backward skew, no messages are dropped early.
promises.workload_sketch: nats stream add L --max-msgs 100 --max-bytes 10KB --max-age 1m; publish continuously; skew clock or kill -9 and restart; poll nats stream info L
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: MaxAge expiry uses message timestamps compared with the wall clock, so a forward skew may mass-expire messages and a backward skew may keep them too long.

promises.quote: The `DiscardOld` option removes old messages making space for new, while `DiscardNew` refuses any new messages.
promises.plain: With DiscardNew at the limit, new publishes get an error and are not stored. With DiscardOld, the oldest messages are removed instead.
promises.when_to_inject: Many concurrent publishers hit a stream sitting just below its limit. Optionally restart the server at the limit.
promises.outside_observation: With DiscardNew: count never exceeds MaxMsgs, every publish that got a positive PubAck is stored, every rejected one is absent, and the earliest messages are kept. With DiscardOld: the newest messages are kept and the first sequence advances.
promises.workload_sketch: nats stream add D --max-msgs 10 --discard new; 50 parallel nats req D.x m$i; nats stream info D; compare the stored sequences with the PubAcks Fuss logged
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the limit check may race with the append, so the stream could overshoot or a positive PubAck could be followed by eviction.

promises.quote: you can say a Stream will only accept messages up to 1024 bytes using `MaxMsgSize`.
promises.plain: Messages larger than MaxMsgSize are rejected and never stored, including after the stream config survives a restart.
promises.when_to_inject: Restart the server, then publish oversized messages.
promises.outside_observation: Oversized publishes get an error PubAck, and no stored message exceeds MaxMsgSize.
promises.workload_sketch: nats stream add S --max-msg-size 1024; restart; nats req S.x <2KB payload>; nats stream info S
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the config reload after restart could drop or default the limit.

promises.quote: So far, all the Consumers you have seen were Durable, meaning they exist even after you disconnect from JetStream.
promises.plain: Durable consumers and their position survive client disconnects and server restarts.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill the server after a durable consumer has delivered and acked part of the stream.
promises.outside_observation: After restart, nats consumer info shows the same consumer with an ack floor at or beyond the last confirmed AckSync. Fetching resumes from there instead of the start.
promises.workload_sketch: nats consumer add ORDERS D --pull --ack explicit; fetch and AckSync 10; kill -9; restart; nats consumer info ORDERS D; nats consumer next ORDERS D
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: consumer state files may be written periodically, so the position could roll back. That would cause redelivery, which is allowed for non-AckSync acks but not for AckSync'd ones.

promises.quote: Regardless of what mode you set, this is only the starting point. Once started it will always give you what you have not seen or acknowledged.
promises.plain: After the start point, a consumer eventually delivers every unacked message and never skips any, including across restarts.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill the server while messages are delivered but not yet acked.
promises.outside_observation: Every stream sequence from the start point onward is delivered at least once and is either acked or still pending. No sequence is missing from Fuss's delivery log, and first deliveries arrive in increasing stream order.
promises.workload_sketch: Publish 1..N; a pull consumer fetches with explicit ack and acks a random subset; kill -9; restart; fetch until empty after AckWait; check coverage of 1..N
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: on recovery, the delivered pointer could be restored ahead of the ack floor without redelivering the pending gap.

promises.quote: In this mode if you acknowledge message `100` it will also acknowledge message `1`-`99`, this is good for processing batches and to reduce ack overhead
promises.plain: With AckAll, acking message N also acks every earlier message, and none of them are redelivered, even after a restart.
promises.when_to_inject: Right after a successful synchronous ack of message 100 on an AckAll consumer.
promises.outside_observation: After restart and once AckWait has passed, none of messages 1-100 are redelivered, and the ack floor is at 100 or higher.
promises.workload_sketch: nats consumer add ORDERS A --pull --ack all; fetch 100; AckSync only the 100th; kill -9; restart; fetch; nats consumer info ORDERS A
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the persisted ack floor might be updated without the range of pending entries, so leftover pending entries come back after restart.

promises.quote: Signals that the message will not be processed now and processing can move onto the next message, NAK'd message will be retried
promises.plain: A NAK'd message is redelivered later, including after a restart.
promises.when_to_inject: After a NAK is sent, before the redelivery happens.
promises.outside_observation: The NAK'd stream sequence is delivered again, with a higher delivery count, after restart.
promises.workload_sketch: Fetch 1; msg.Nak() with a reply; kill -9; restart; fetch and check that the same stream sequence returns
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a NAK might be treated as a final state in persisted state and get lost.

promises.quote: When sent before the AckWait period indicates that work is ongoing and the period should be extended by another equal to `AckWait`
promises.plain: A progress ack pushes back redelivery by one more AckWait.
promises.when_to_inject: Jump the wall clock forward just after a +WPI is sent.
promises.outside_observation: No redelivery to other fetchers within AckWait (by Fuss's monotonic clock) after the +WPI. Redelivery does happen after the extension expires with no further progress acks.
promises.workload_sketch: Consumer with --wait 10s; fetch; at 8s send msg.InProgress(); skew clock +1h; a second fetcher polls; record the redelivery time
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: AckWait deadlines may be computed from the wall clock, so a forward skew could trigger an early redelivery.

promises.quote: Instructs the server to stop redelivery of a message without acknowledging it as successfully processed
promises.plain: After AckTerm, the message is never redelivered, even after a restart.
promises.when_to_inject: After a successful synchronous AckTerm.
promises.outside_observation: The terminated sequence is never delivered again after restart and AckWait.
promises.workload_sketch: Fetch 1; msg.Term() with a reply subject and wait for the reply; kill -9; restart; fetch until empty
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a terminated message might be recorded in memory only and lost on crash.

promises.quote: All of these acknowledgement modes, except `AckNext`, support double acknowledgement - if you set a reply subject when acknowledging the server will in turn acknowledge having received your ACK.
promises.plain: The server confirms each ack that carries a reply subject, and a confirmed ack takes effect durably.
promises.when_to_inject: Right after the server's confirmation of an ack, NAK, or term arrives.
promises.outside_observation: The confirmed effect (acked, terminated, or NAK'd) is reflected in consumer behavior after restart.
promises.workload_sketch: For each ack type, send it with a reply subject and wait; kill -9; restart; observe redelivery behavior
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the confirmation may be sent before the state is persisted.

promises.quote: The Consumer sequence increases - each delivery attempt increases the sequence - and our redelivered count also goes up.
promises.plain: Consumer sequence numbers only increase with each delivery attempt and never repeat or go backward, including across restarts.
promises.when_to_inject: Restart between delivery attempts of an unacked message.
promises.outside_observation: The consumer sequences in message metadata that Fuss logs are strictly increasing across the restart. Redelivered messages carry a growing delivery count.
promises.workload_sketch: Fetch with --no-ack several times while logging the metadata (consumer seq, num delivered); kill -9; restart; fetch again and compare
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: if the delivered sequence persisted on disk lags the in-memory value, consumer sequences could be reused after a crash.

promises.quote: An Ephemeral Consumer exists as long as any subscription is active on its delivery subject. It is automatically be removed, after a short grace period to handle restarts, when there are no subscribers.
promises.plain: An ephemeral consumer stays alive while it has a subscriber, survives brief interruptions, and is cleaned up after a grace period with no subscribers.
promises.when_to_inject: Restart the server, or disconnect and reconnect the subscriber briefly, while an ephemeral consumer is active.
promises.outside_observation: nats consumer ls shows the ephemeral consumer still present during the grace period and gone some time after its last subscriber leaves.
promises.workload_sketch: nats sub my.monitor; nats consumer add ORDERS --ephemeral --target my.monitor --ack none; restart the server; check nats consumer ls; kill the sub; wait; check nats consumer ls again
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the grace-period timer could be reset or lost on restart, leaking consumers or removing them too early.

promises.quote: You might want to replay messages at the rate they arrived though, meaning if messages first arrived 1 minute apart, and you make a new Consumer it will get the messages a minute apart.
promises.plain: A ReplayOriginal consumer reproduces the original gaps between messages.
promises.when_to_inject: Step the wall clock during a replay.
promises.outside_observation: The gaps between deliveries, measured on Fuss's monotonic clock, match the gaps between stored timestamps.
promises.workload_sketch: Publish 3 messages 10s apart; nats consumer add ... --replay original --target out; nats sub out; skew the clock mid-replay; record arrival times
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: replay pacing may use wall-clock deltas, so a skew could cause bursts or long stalls.

promises.quote: Delivers from a specific time onward. Requires `OptStartTime` to be set
promises.plain: A by_start_time consumer starts at the first message stored at or after the given time.
promises.when_to_inject: Skew the server clock backward between publishes so stored timestamps go out of order, then create the consumer.
promises.outside_observation: The first delivered message matches what Fuss expects from its own publish log and the stored timestamps. Check for skipped or extra messages.
promises.workload_sketch: Publish m1; skew clock -5m; publish m2 and m3; nats consumer add ORDERS T --pull --deliver <time> ; nats consumer next ORDERS T
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the start-time lookup may assume timestamps increase with sequence and binary-search incorrectly when they don't.

promises.quote: We do store some message data with each message, namely: * Message headers * The subject it was received on * The time it was received * The message payload * A hash of the message * The message sequence
promises.plain: Each stored record carries a hash and sequence, so a torn write from a crash can be detected and is not served as a valid message.
promises.when_to_inject: Fill the disk, or kill the process, mid-append during heavy publishing.
promises.outside_observation: After restart, no message is served with a corrupted body or subject, and every acked message is intact. Fuss can also read the block files read-only and verify record framing.
promises.workload_sketch: Fill the filesystem to near capacity; publish large messages in a loop via nats req; kill -9 or let ENOSPC hit; free space; restart; nats stream get every sequence and compare with the publish log
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: recovery may truncate at the first bad record and lose later acked records, or skip the hash check.

promises.quote:
NATS will create replacement stream replicas automatically under the following conditions:

* Impacted stream is of replica configuration R3 (or greater)
* Remaining intact nodes (stream replicas) meet minimum RAFT quorum: floor(R/2) + 1
* Available node(s) in the stream's cluster for new replica(s)
* Impacted node(s) removed from the stream's domain RAFT Meta group (e.g. `nats server cluster peer-remove`)
promises.plain: If an R3+ stream loses a node but keeps quorum, and a spare node exists and the dead node is peer-removed, JetStream automatically builds a replacement replica.
promises.when_to_inject: Permanently kill one replica's server while publishes are still being acknowledged. Then run peer-remove while the cluster is still under publish load.
promises.outside_observation: `nats stream info` should eventually list a new replica on the spare node with current=true. Every message Fuss recorded as acked must be readable from the stream, with the same sequence and payload. This must still hold after the original leader is later killed.
promises.workload_sketch: Start 4 servers. `nats stream add S --replicas 3 --storage file`. Publish N numbered messages and log each ack. Kill one replica's process and never restart it. Run `nats server cluster peer-remove <name>`. Keep publishing. Poll `nats stream info S`. Read every sequence with `nats stream get` and compare against the ack log.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: catch-up to the new replica could race with ongoing writes or a leader change, leaving the new replica with gaps. A later failover to that replica would then lose acked messages.

promises.quote: Remaining intact nodes (stream replicas) meet minimum RAFT quorum: floor(R/2) + 1
promises.plain: Automatic recovery depends on quorum. If quorum is lost, the stream should not silently invent replicas or accept writes it cannot replicate.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill two of three replicas of an R3 stream, then peer-remove them.
promises.outside_observation: Publishes should fail or time out rather than be acked. No replacement replicas should appear until quorum returns. After the killed nodes restart, no acked message may be missing.
promises.workload_sketch: R3 stream on a 5-node cluster. Publish and log acks. Kill 2 replicas. Attempt publishes and record whether each was acked or errored. Run peer-remove on the killed nodes. Watch `nats stream info`. Restart the nodes. Verify the full ack log against stream contents.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the remaining minority replica might acknowledge writes or get promoted, causing acked-then-lost messages once the majority returns.

promises.quote:
The backup includes (by default):

* Stream configuration and state
* Stream durable consumer configuration and state
* All message payload data including metadata like timestamps and headers
promises.plain: A stream backup restored elsewhere reproduces the stream's config, durable consumer config and positions, and every message with its timestamp and headers.
promises.when_to_inject: After the backup completes, kill the source server and restore onto a fresh server with an empty storage directory.
promises.outside_observation: Compare the restored stream with Fuss's pre-backup history. Check `nats stream info` config and state (first/last sequence, message count). Check `nats consumer info` ack floor and delivered sequence. Check each message's subject, payload, headers and timestamp via `nats stream get`.
promises.workload_sketch: Create a file stream and a durable consumer. Publish N messages with unique headers. Consume and ack the first K. Record everything. Run `nats stream backup S dir`. Kill the server. Start a new server. Run `nats stream restore dir`. Diff the restored state against the record. Then fetch from the consumer and confirm the next delivery is K+1.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: consumer state may be snapshotted at a slightly different moment than the stream data, so restored ack floors could lag and cause redeliveries, or run ahead and skip messages.

promises.quote:
During a backup operation, the stream is placed in a status where it's configuration cannot change and no data will be
evicted based on stream retention policies.
promises.plain: While a backup runs, stream config edits are refused and retention-based deletion is paused.
promises.when_to_inject: Mid-backup, while the progress bar or log lines show chunks still being transferred.
promises.outside_observation: `nats stream edit` during the backup should fail, or at least the config must not change. With limits like max-msgs, max-age or work-queue retention, `nats stream info` first-sequence must not advance during the backup. The backup must contain every message present at backup start.
promises.workload_sketch: Create a stream with `--max-msgs` small and `--max-age 2s`, filled near the limit with large payloads so the backup is slow. Start `nats stream backup S dir --no-progress`. Concurrently publish past the limit, run `nats stream edit S --max-msgs X`, and poll `nats stream info` first-seq. After the backup, restore to a new server and check its contents.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the age-based expiry timer or limit enforcement on publish might not check the backup status, so messages are evicted during the snapshot.

promises.quote: An existing backup (as above) can be restored to the same or a new NATS server (or cluster) using the `nats stream restore` command.
promises.plain: A backup restores correctly onto the original server or a different server or cluster, and the restored stream survives restart.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill the target server right after `nats stream restore` reports success. A second variant kills it mid-restore.
promises.outside_observation: After restart, a restore that reported success must have its full contents present. A restore killed partway must either leave no stream or a stream that is visibly not fully restored, never a stream silently missing messages. Fuss can check this with `nats stream ls`, `nats stream info` and message reads.
promises.workload_sketch: Back up stream S. On a target server, run `nats stream restore dir`. Kill -9 either after success or mid-progress. Restart the server. Run `nats stream info S` and read all messages. Compare with the backup's recorded state.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: restored data may be acknowledged before it is fsynced, or a half-restored stream may be registered as a normal stream after restart.

promises.quote: The `nats account backup` and `nats account restore` commands allow you to back up and restore all streams in an account at once, including their configuration, consumer state, and all message data.
promises.plain: Account backup and restore captures and reproduces every stream in the account, with config, consumer state and messages.
promises.when_to_inject: Between backup and restore, kill the source server and use a fresh server. A variant kills the target mid account-restore.
promises.outside_observation: Every stream recorded by Fuss must exist on the target after restore. Each must match Fuss's recorded config, message contents and consumer positions. Each stream must appear as its own subdirectory in the backup directory, which Fuss can read.
promises.workload_sketch: Create 3 file streams with durable consumers and partial acks. Log all of it. Run `nats account backup dir --consumers`. List the subdirectories in dir. Kill the server. Start a fresh server. Run `nats account restore dir`. Diff each stream and consumer.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: per-stream backups are taken sequentially, so streams can be captured at different points in time. A crash mid account-restore may leave only some streams restored, with no clear indication.

promises.quote: `nats account restore` will fail if a stream with the same name already exists. You must remove the existing stream before restoring from backup.
promises.plain: Restoring over an existing stream name fails instead of overwriting or merging.
promises.when_to_inject: Run two `nats account restore` processes on the same backup simultaneously, and separately restore while a same-named stream exists.
promises.outside_observation: For an existing stream, the restore must error, and the stream's messages and sequence numbers must be unchanged. For concurrent restores, exactly one should create each stream. There must be no duplicated or interleaved messages and no corrupted state.
promises.workload_sketch: Create stream S with known messages. Run `nats account restore dir`, where dir contains S, and expect failure. Verify S is unchanged. Delete S. Launch two `nats account restore dir` at once. Check the resulting S against the backup contents.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the existence check and stream creation may not be atomic, so two concurrent restores could both pass the check and interleave their data.

promises.quote: | `--check` | Check backup integrity |
promises.plain: Backing up with --check detects a corrupt or incomplete backup.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill the nats-server mid `nats account backup --check`, or kill the CLI process mid-backup.
promises.outside_observation: An interrupted backup must not be reported as a successful, checked backup. A later restore from it must either fail or produce the correct data, never silently truncated data.
promises.workload_sketch: Fill a large stream. Start `nats account backup dir --check --no-progress`. Kill the server partway. Record the CLI exit code and output. Attempt `nats account restore dir` on a fresh server and compare the result against the record.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the integrity check may verify only chunks received, not the expected total, so a truncated snapshot could pass.

promises.quote: A _mirror_ copies data from 1 other stream, as far as possible IDs and ordering will match exactly the source.
promises.plain: A mirror holds the origin stream's messages in the same order and, where possible, with the same sequence numbers.
promises.when_to_inject: While a steady publish loop into the origin stream is running and the mirror is actively catching up (mirror Lag > 0). Kill the server hosting the mirror, or the origin's leader, then restart it.
promises.outside_observation: After publishing stops and mirror Lag reaches 0, read both streams in full with an ordered consumer or direct get. Compare the (stream sequence, payload) lists. The mirror should be an exact prefix-equal copy, with no gaps, no reordering, and no duplicated payloads. Also check for sequence-number drift against Fuss's own log of acked publishes.
promises.workload_sketch: nats s add SRC --subjects 'src.>' --storage file; nats s add MIR --mirror SRC --storage file; loop: nats req src.x 'msg {{Count}}' --count 5000 (record each ack seq to the Fuss log); kill -9 the nats-server mid-loop; restart it with the same config; wait until `nats s info MIR` shows Lag 0; dump both streams with `nats s get` or a consumer and diff them.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the mirror's consumer position on the origin may be persisted separately from the mirror's own store. A crash between the two could make it re-fetch messages (duplicates or shifted sequences) or skip a range (gap).

promises.quote: A _mirror_ does not listen on a subject for any data to be added.
promises.plain: Only data copied from the origin ever appears in a mirror; nothing published directly to subjects ends up in it.
promises.when_to_inject: After the mirror is created, restart the server. Then publish on the origin's subjects and on other arbitrary subjects.
promises.outside_observation: The mirror's message count and contents equal exactly the origin's, before and after the restart. No extra messages appear, and no publish to a subject is acked by the mirror stream name.
promises.workload_sketch: nats s add SRC --subjects 'src.>'; nats s add MIR --mirror SRC; restart nats-server; nats req src.a x --count 10; nats pub mir.anything y; check that the stream name in each publish ack is never MIR; compare `nats s info MIR` msg count with SRC.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: on config reload after restart, the mirror config could be re-applied incorrectly and the stream could gain a subject binding.

promises.quote: A _mirror_ can filter by subject and the Start Sequence and Start Time can be set.
promises.plain: A mirror with a subject filter or start point copies only matching messages from that start point onward, and this keeps working across restarts.
promises.when_to_inject: Create a mirror with a Start Time while the server clock is skewed forward or backward relative to the message timestamps. Also skew the clock and restart the server while the mirror is still catching up.
promises.outside_observation: The mirror should contain exactly the origin messages whose stored timestamp is at or after Start Time (or whose sequence is at or after Start Sequence) and that match the filter. Watch for messages before the start appearing after a restart, or for valid messages missing.
promises.workload_sketch: Publish 1000 msgs to SRC on subjects src.a and src.b, recording ack times; create MIR with --mirror SRC, start time T (the midpoint), and filter src.a; start the server under libfaketime offset ±1h; restart mid catch-up; compare MIR contents to the expected set computed from the Fuss log.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: if resume after restart re-evaluates Start Time against wall-clock 'now' rather than stored message timestamps, skew could cause re-copying or skipping.

promises.quote: A _source_ is a stream where data is copied from, one stream can have multiple sources and will read data in from them all.
promises.plain: A sourced stream eventually holds every message from every one of its sources.
promises.when_to_inject: While publishing concurrently into two source streams and the aggregate stream is pulling from both. Kill the server or cluster node hosting the aggregate stream, then restart it.
promises.outside_observation: Once Lag is 0 for every source in `nats s info ARCHIVE` (or `nats s report`), the set of payloads in ARCHIVE should equal the union of acked payloads in ORDERS and RETURNS. The count should be exact, with nothing missing and nothing duplicated.
promises.workload_sketch: Use file storage for ORDERS and RETURNS so kills don't legitimately lose source data. nats s add ARCHIVE --source ORDERS --source RETURNS --storage file; run two concurrent loops: nats req ORDERS.new 'ORDER {{Count}}' --count 2000 and nats req RETURNS.new 'RETURN {{Count}}' --count 2000; kill -9 mid-run; restart; wait for Lag 0; assert ARCHIVE msg count = 4000 and the payload sets match.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the per-source last-seen sequence may not be fsynced together with the copied messages. That could lose a tail or duplicate one after a crash.

promises.quote: We can therefore not maintain absolute ordering, but data from 1 single source will be in the correct order but mixed in with other streams.
promises.plain: In a sourced stream, messages from any single source keep their original relative order, even though they are interleaved with other sources.
promises.when_to_inject: During concurrent catch-up from multiple sources. Kill and restart the aggregate stream's server, ideally more than once.
promises.outside_observation: Read ARCHIVE in sequence order and project it per source, using a payload prefix such as 'ORDER n' or 'RETURN n'. Each projection's counter must be strictly increasing with no repeats.
