promises.workload_sketch: As in the previous workload, with payloads carrying a per-source monotonic counter; kill -9 the server twice during catch-up; after Lag reaches 0, consume ARCHIVE with an ordered consumer and check monotonicity per source.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: on resume, a source could be re-fetched from an earlier sequence. Re-delivered older messages would then land after newer ones and break per-source order.

promises.quote: The stream will also listen for messages on it's own subject.
promises.plain: A sourced stream that has its own subjects also stores messages published directly to it, alongside sourced data.
promises.when_to_inject: While publishing directly to the sourced stream's own subject and also into its sources at the same time. Kill and restart the server.
promises.outside_observation: Every direct publish acked with stream=ARCHIVE is present in ARCHIVE after restart. Sourced messages are also all present, and the total equals direct acks plus source acks.
promises.workload_sketch: nats s add ARCHIVE --source ORDERS --source RETURNS --subjects 'archive.>' --storage file; run concurrently: nats req archive.direct 'D {{Count}}' --count 1000 and nats req ORDERS.new 'O {{Count}}' --count 1000; kill -9 mid-run; restart; verify that all acked D and O payloads are present exactly once.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: direct publishes and sourced writes may race on the same store. A crash could leave an acked direct publish unpersisted, or interleave writes inconsistently.

promises.quote: A source can have Start Time or Start Sequence and can filter by a subject.
promises.plain: A source configured with a start point and a subject filter copies only matching messages from that point on, and keeps doing so across restarts.
promises.when_to_inject: Restart the server after the sourced stream has partially caught up from a source that has a Start Sequence and a filter.
promises.outside_observation: ARCHIVE should contain only source messages with sequence at or after Start Sequence that match the filter, each exactly once. A restart must not cause messages before the start, or non-matching messages, to appear.
promises.workload_sketch: Publish 1000 msgs to ORDERS on ORDERS.new and ORDERS.cancel; create ARCHIVE with source ORDERS, start sequence 500, filter ORDERS.new; restart nats-server mid catch-up; compare ARCHIVE to the expected subset from the Fuss log.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: after a restart, the source consumer might be recreated from the configured Start Sequence instead of its last processed position, re-copying already-copied messages.

promises.quote: The _REPORT_ Stream does not listen for any incoming messages, it can only consume data from _ARCHIVE_.
promises.plain: A chained mirror (mirroring a sourced stream) contains exactly what its origin has, and nothing else.
promises.when_to_inject: While data flows ORDERS/RETURNS → ARCHIVE → REPORT. Kill the server hosting ARCHIVE, the intermediate hop, then restart it.
promises.outside_observation: After all Lags reach 0, REPORT should equal ARCHIVE message-for-message in order, and ARCHIVE should equal the union of the sources.
promises.workload_sketch: Create ORDERS and RETURNS as file streams; nats s add ARCHIVE --source ORDERS --source RETURNS; nats s add REPORT --mirror ARCHIVE; publish 100+100 as in the spec, scaled to thousands; kill -9 the ARCHIVE host mid-flow; restart; diff REPORT against ARCHIVE.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: if ARCHIVE re-copies a duplicate after its crash, REPORT will faithfully mirror the duplicate, and the error propagates down the chain.

promises.quote: We can now see from a Stream Report that the data has been replicated:
promises.plain: After writing 100 messages to each of two sources, the sourced stream ends with exactly 200 messages and its mirror with exactly 200, with 0 lost.
promises.when_to_inject: In the middle of the two `nats req --count 100` runs. Kill the server hosting ARCHIVE or REPORT, then restart it.
promises.outside_observation: `nats s report` shows ARCHIVE = REPORT = the number of acked publishes to the sources, the Lost column is 0, and the replication report has Lag 0 with an empty Error column.
promises.workload_sketch: Replicate the spec setup with file-backed sources; nats req ORDERS.new 'ORDER {{Count}}' --count 100 & nats req RETURNS.new 'RETURN {{Count}}' --count 100; kill -9 during the runs; restart; poll `nats s report` until Lag 0; compare counts to the Fuss ack log.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: counts may converge to more than 200 because of re-fetch duplicates after a crash, since the spec does not say sourcing is deduplicated.

promises.quote: Here the `Lag` is how far behind we were reported as being last time we saw a message.
promises.plain: The reported Lag reflects how far the mirror or source is behind, and returns to 0 once caught up.
promises.when_to_inject: While the mirror is behind. Restart the mirror's server and watch Lag during and after recovery.
promises.outside_observation: Lag decreases to 0 after recovery, and Lag 0 coincides with the mirror message count equaling the origin's. Watch for Lag 0 reported while messages are still missing.
promises.workload_sketch: Stop the mirror's server; publish 5000 msgs to the origin; start the mirror's server; poll `nats s info MIR` every 200ms, logging Lag and message counts to Fuss; check that Lag 0 implies equal counts.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: per the wording, Lag is the value from the last message seen, so it may be stale. It could read 0 right after a restart before any fetch has happened.

promises.quote: You can do a normal publish to the subject for unacknowledged delivery, though it’s better to use the JetStream publish calls instead as the JetStream server will reply with an acknowledgement that it was successfully stored.
promises.plain: A message the server has acknowledged on a JetStream publish is stored and stays readable after a crash and restart.
promises.when_to_inject: Send SIGKILL to nats-server right after a stream of acked publishes, ideally within milliseconds of the last ack.
promises.outside_observation: Fuss logs every PubAck (stream and sequence) to its own history file. After restart, Fuss reads the stream back with an ordered consumer or direct get. Every acked sequence must exist with the same subject and payload.
promises.workload_sketch: nats stream add S --subjects 'o.>' --storage file --replicas 1; loop: js.Publish('o.N', payload N) and record the ack seq; kill -9 the server; restart it with the same config; nats stream view S, or fetch seq 1..max; diff against the history.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the default sync interval may let the server ack before the data is fsynced. A kill -9 alone leaves the OS page cache intact, so to see real loss Fuss may need to stop the whole VM or container or drop the page cache. A plain process kill may never show it. Fuss can only set the sync interval through documented config.

promises.quote: You can do a normal publish to the subject for unacknowledged delivery, though it’s better to use the JetStream publish calls instead as the JetStream server will reply with an acknowledgement that it was successfully stored.
promises.plain: When the disk fills up, the server must not ack a publish it could not durably store.
promises.when_to_inject: Fill the filesystem that holds the JetStream store directory partway through a publish loop.
promises.outside_observation: Every publish that got a positive PubAck must be readable after space is freed and the server restarts. Publishes that failed or timed out may be present or absent, but none may be present more than once or corrupted.
promises.workload_sketch: Use a small loopback or tmpfs filesystem as store_dir. Publish in a loop and record ack or error per message. Run fallocate to fill the disk. Keep publishing for a while, then free space, restart the server, and read the whole stream back.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a partial block write on ENOSPC could leave a torn record, so recovery truncates past messages that were already acked.

promises.quote: Streams support deduplication using a `Nats-Msg-Id` header and a sliding window within which to track duplicate messages.
promises.plain: Republishing the same Nats-Msg-Id inside the duplicate window stores the message only once, including when the publish is retried after a crash.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill the server after a publish is sent but before or just after its ack arrives. The client then retries with the same Msg-Id after restart, still inside the window.
promises.outside_observation: Count stored messages carrying each Msg-Id. There must be at most one per Msg-Id. The retry's PubAck should report duplicate=true, or the same sequence as the original.
promises.workload_sketch: nats stream add S --subjects 'd.>' --dupe-window 2m; for i: publish with header Nats-Msg-Id=id-i; kill -9 at random; restart; republish every id whose ack was unknown or seen; read the stream and group by Msg-Id.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the duplicate-tracking state may be rebuilt from disk on restart only partially, or may live only in memory, so a retry after restart gets stored a second time.

promises.quote: Upon reaching message limits, the server will automatically discard messages either by removing the oldest messages to make room for new ones (`DiscardOld`) or by refusing to store new messages (`DiscardNew`).
promises.plain: With DiscardNew, the stream never holds more than its limit and extra publishes are refused. With DiscardOld, only the oldest messages are removed.
promises.when_to_inject: Run many concurrent publishers while the stream sits right at its limit, optionally with a process kill in the middle.
promises.outside_observation: DiscardNew: the number of acked messages is at most MaxMsgs, and every acked message is still present. DiscardOld: the surviving messages are exactly the newest MaxMsgs by sequence, with no gaps in the middle.
promises.workload_sketch: nats stream add S --max-msgs 100 --discard new; run 20 goroutines that publish 50 messages each; record acks and errors; read the stream; repeat with --discard old.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the limit check and the append race under concurrency, so the stream briefly or permanently goes over the limit, or acks a message it then drops.

promises.quote: Maximum number of messages stored in the stream. Adheres to Discard Policy, removing oldest or refusing new messages if the Stream exceeds this number of messages.
promises.plain: The MaxMsgs limit is still enforced correctly after a crash and restart.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill the server while publishes are pushing the stream over MaxMsgs, then restart it.
promises.outside_observation: After restart, nats stream info shows a message count at or below MaxMsgs. The first and last sequences agree with the history: newest kept for DiscardOld, no acked message missing for DiscardNew.
promises.workload_sketch: nats stream add S --max-msgs 1000 --discard old; publish 5000 messages; kill -9 midway; restart; nats stream info S; read the first and last sequences.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: recovery rebuilds the message count from block files and may count messages that were deleted but not yet compacted.

promises.quote: Maximum number of bytes stored in the stream. Adheres to Discard Policy, removing oldest or refusing new messages if the Stream exceeds this size.
promises.plain: Stream bytes never exceed MaxBytes, under load and after restart.
promises.when_to_inject: Run concurrent large publishes near the byte limit, followed by a restart.
promises.outside_observation: The bytes reported by nats stream info stay at or below MaxBytes. With DiscardNew, every acked message is still present.
promises.workload_sketch: nats stream add S --max-bytes 1MB --discard new; publish 10KB messages from 10 clients concurrently; record acks; restart; check stream info and read back.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: byte accounting may be done after the append, which allows an overshoot under concurrency.

promises.quote: For example, if `MaxAge` is set to one minute, the server will automatically delete messages older than one minute with this policy.
promises.plain: Messages are removed once they are older than MaxAge, and not removed before that.
promises.when_to_inject: Step the server host clock forward by a large amount, and separately backward, while the stream holds messages of known age.
promises.outside_observation: Fuss checks the stored message timestamps and its own wall-clock record. It flags messages deleted well before MaxAge by real elapsed time, and messages that survive far past MaxAge after a backward jump.
promises.workload_sketch: nats stream add S --max-age 1m; publish 100 messages; jump the server clock +2h with faketime or date -s; poll stream info for the message count; repeat with a -2h jump and wait 2 real minutes.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: expiry compares stored wall-clock timestamps with the current wall clock, so a forward jump instantly purges fresh data and a backward jump keeps data forever.

promises.quote: `WorkQueuePolicy` - Retention with the typical behavior of a FIFO queue. Each message can be consumed only once. This is enforced by only allowing _one_ consumer to be created _per subject_ for a work-queue stream (i.e. the consumers' subject filter(s) must _not_ overlap). Once a given message is ack’ed, it will be deleted from the stream.
promises.plain: In a work-queue stream, a message whose ack was confirmed is deleted and never delivered again, even across crashes.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill the server just after the consumer sends an ack, especially a double-ack, i.e. AckSync, that the server confirmed.
promises.outside_observation: Fuss records each message whose AckSync succeeded. After restart, none of those may be redelivered, and none may appear in the stream when read with direct get by sequence.
promises.workload_sketch: nats stream add Q --retention work --subjects 'q.>'; nats consumer add Q W --pull --ack explicit; publish 1000 messages; fetch and AckSync in a loop; kill -9 at random; restart; keep fetching; check for redelivery of confirmed-acked sequences.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the ack is applied to consumer state but the stream-side delete is flushed later, so after a crash the message comes back as pending.

promises.quote: Each message can be consumed only once. This is enforced by only allowing _one_ consumer to be created _per subject_ for a work-queue stream (i.e. the consumers' subject filter(s) must _not_ overlap).
promises.plain: The server refuses to create overlapping consumers on a work-queue stream, even when the create requests are concurrent.
promises.when_to_inject: Send many consumer-create requests with overlapping filters at the same moment.
promises.outside_observation: At most one of the overlapping consumers succeeds. nats consumer ls shows no two consumers with overlapping filters, before and after restart.
promises.workload_sketch: nats stream add Q --retention work --subjects 'q.>'; from 10 clients at once, nats consumer add Q Ci --filter 'q.>'; list consumers; restart; list again.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the overlap check and the consumer registration are not done under one lock, so two creates both pass the check.

promises.quote: Messages that have attempted redelivery and have reached `MaxDeliver` attempts for the consumer will remain in the stream and must be manually deleted via the JetStream API.
promises.plain: Messages that ran out of MaxDeliver attempts on a work-queue stream are not dropped, including across restarts.
promises.when_to_inject: Restart the server after messages have hit MaxDeliver without being acked.
promises.outside_observation: Direct get by sequence still returns those messages after restart, and nats stream info counts them.
promises.workload_sketch: nats stream add Q --retention work; nats consumer add Q W --pull --max-deliver 2 --ack-wait 1s; publish 10 messages; fetch them twice and never ack; restart; get each sequence directly.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: recovery may treat max-delivered messages like acked ones and remove them.

promises.quote: Once a given message is ack’ed by _all_ consumers filtering on the subject, the message is deleted (same behavior as `WorkQueuePolicy`).
promises.plain: An interest-policy message is kept until every interested consumer acks it, and is not deleted early even after a crash.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill the server after one of two consumers has acked a message but before the second has.
promises.outside_observation: After restart, the second consumer still receives every message it never acked. No message is lost while any consumer still has interest in it.
promises.workload_sketch: nats stream add I --retention interest --subjects 'i.>'; add durable pull consumers A and B; publish 500 messages; A fetches and acks all; kill -9; restart; B fetches everything and Fuss checks that all 500 arrive.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: after restart, interest state is rebuilt from a stale consumer snapshot, so messages look fully acked and get deleted.

promises.quote: Sealed streams do not allow messages to be deleted via limits or API, sealed streams can not be unsealed via configuration update.
promises.plain: Once a stream is sealed, no message disappears and the seal holds across restarts.
promises.when_to_inject: Seal the stream, then kill and restart the server. Also inject a clock jump past MaxAge.
promises.outside_observation: The message set is identical before and after the restart and the clock jump. Delete, purge and unseal requests are all refused.
promises.workload_sketch: nats stream add S --max-age 1m; publish 100 messages; nats stream seal S; kill -9; restart; jump the clock +1h; read all messages; try nats stream rmm and nats stream purge.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the age-expiry timer runs during recovery before the sealed flag is loaded.

promises.quote: Restricts the ability to delete messages from a stream via the API.
promises.plain: With DenyDelete set, message delete calls are refused, including after a restart.
promises.when_to_inject: Restart the server after creating the stream with DenyDelete, then issue delete calls.
promises.outside_observation: Delete API calls return an error and the message is still readable.
promises.workload_sketch: nats stream add S --deny-delete; publish; kill -9; restart; nats stream rmm S 1; nats stream get S 1.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the flag may not persist into the stream metadata file that is reloaded on restart.

promises.quote: Restricts the ability to purge messages from a stream via the API.
promises.plain: With DenyPurge set, purge calls are refused, including after a restart.
promises.when_to_inject: Restart the server after creating the stream with DenyPurge, then issue purge calls.
promises.outside_observation: The purge call errors and the message count is unchanged.
promises.workload_sketch: nats stream add S --deny-purge; publish 100 messages; kill -9; restart; nats stream purge S -f; nats stream info S.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: same as DenyDelete, the config flag may be lost on reload.

promises.quote: If set, allows atomically writing a batch of N messages into the stream.
promises.plain: An atomic batch is either stored completely or not at all, even if the server is killed mid-batch.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill the server after some of the batch messages have been sent but before the commit message, and also right after the commit is sent.
promises.outside_observation: After restart, each batch id has either all N of its messages, in order and contiguous, or none of them. A batch whose commit was acked must be fully present.
promises.workload_sketch: nats stream add S --allow-batch (AllowAtomicPublish=true); a client publishes N messages carrying the Nats-Batch-Id / Nats-Batch-Sequence headers and a commit header on the last one; kill -9 at random points; restart; read and group by batch id.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the batch is staged and then applied as several appends, so a crash during the apply leaves a prefix of the batch on disk.

promises.quote: The `Nats-Rollup: all` header will purge all prior messages in the stream. Whereas the `sub` value will purge all prior messages for a given subject.
promises.plain: After an acked rollup, the older messages in its scope are gone and do not come back after a crash.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill the server immediately after the rollup publish is acked.
promises.outside_observation: After restart, only the rollup message and later messages remain in scope (the whole stream for all, the subject for sub). The rollup message itself is present.
promises.workload_sketch: nats stream add S --allow-rollup; publish 100 messages on s.a; publish with header Nats-Rollup: sub on s.a; kill -9; restart; read all s.a messages.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the purge is recorded lazily as tombstones, and a crash replays the old blocks without them.

promises.quote: If enabled, the `RePublish` stream option will result in the server re-publishing messages received into a stream automatically and immediately after a successful write, to a distinct destination subject.
promises.plain: A message only gets republished after it has been written, so every republished message must be in the stream, and republish order follows stream order.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill the server while publishes and republishes are flowing.
promises.outside_observation: Fuss subscribes to the destination and logs each republished message's Nats-Sequence header. After restart, every logged sequence must exist in the stream with the same data, and the logged sequences must be strictly increasing.
promises.workload_sketch: nats stream add S --subjects 'r.>' with republish src 'r.>' dest 'rp.>'; nats sub 'rp.>' and log it; publish in a loop; kill -9; restart; compare the log to the stream contents.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the republish fires after the in-memory append but before the data is durable, so a crash leaves republished messages that the stream no longer has.

promises.quote: When a stream is configured with a `source` or `mirror`, it will automatically and asynchronously replicate messages from the origin stream.
promises.plain: A mirror eventually holds every origin message in the same order, without duplicates, even if the server restarts during replication.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill and restart the server while the mirror is catching up on a large backlog.
promises.outside_observation: Once publishing stops and things settle, the mirror's messages match the origin's one-for-one, with the same order and payloads and no duplicates or gaps.
promises.workload_sketch: nats stream add O --subjects 'o.>'; nats stream add M --mirror O; publish 10000 messages to O; kill -9 during the mirror's catch-up; restart; wait; compare O and M message by message.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the mirror's record of its last origin sequence is persisted separately from its data, so after a crash it re-fetches or skips a range.

promises.quote: Changes to the source or mirror, e.g. deleting messages or publishing, do not reflect on the origin stream.
promises.plain: Deleting or publishing on a sourcing stream never changes the origin stream, including across restarts.
promises.when_to_inject: Restart after deleting messages from the mirror or source stream.
promises.outside_observation: The origin's message set and sequences are unchanged. The mirror does not re-pull the messages that were deleted from it.
promises.workload_sketch: Set up O and mirror M; publish 100 messages; nats stream rmm M 5; kill -9; restart; read O (all 100 present) and M.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: on restart, the mirror might rewind and re-fetch the deleted messages.

promises.quote: Limits maximum number of messages in the stream to retain _per subject_.
promises.plain: Each subject keeps at most MaxMsgsPerSubject messages, the newest ones, under concurrency and after restart.
promises.when_to_inject: Run concurrent publishes to the same subject, then kill and restart.
promises.outside_observation: For each subject, the stored count is at most the limit, and the stored messages are the latest acked ones for that subject.
promises.workload_sketch: nats stream add S --max-msgs-per-subject 3; 10 clients publish to s.k concurrently; kill -9; restart; nats stream subjects S and read s.k.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the per-subject index is rebuilt on recovery and miscounts, so old entries stay.

promises.quote: If true, applies discard new semantics on a per subject basis. Requires `DiscardPolicy` to be `DiscardNew` and the `MaxMsgsPerSubject` to be set.
promises.plain: Once a subject is full, new publishes to that subject are refused and the existing ones are kept.
promises.when_to_inject: Run concurrent publishes to a subject that is at its per-subject limit.
promises.outside_observation: Acked messages for the subject never exceed the limit, and all acked messages are still present.
promises.workload_sketch: nats stream add S --discard new --discard-per-subject --max-msgs-per-subject 1; 20 clients publish to s.k concurrently; count acks; read s.k.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a check-then-append race lets two publishes both succeed.

promises.quote: If set, a subject delete marker will be placed after the last message of a subject ages out.
promises.plain: When the last message of a subject expires, a delete marker shows up for that subject.
promises.when_to_inject: Jump the server clock forward past MaxAge, and separately restart the server across the expiry moment.
promises.outside_observation: Exactly one marker message appears for each subject whose last message expired. No marker appears while a live message still exists.
promises.workload_sketch: nats stream add S --max-age 30s --subject-delete-marker-ttl 1m (with AllowMsgTTL); publish one message per subject; wait or jump the clock; read the stream and look for markers.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: expiry handled during recovery may skip writing markers, or write duplicate markers.

promises.quote: If set, allows message scheduling in the stream.
promises.plain: Scheduled messages are delivered at their scheduled time, exactly once, even across restarts.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill the server shortly before a schedule's due time and restart it after that time. Also apply clock skew.
promises.outside_observation: Each scheduled message appears in the stream exactly once, not before its due time by Fuss's clock, and not lost across the restart.
promises.workload_sketch: nats stream add S with AllowMsgSchedules; publish schedule messages due in 30s using the documented schedule headers; kill -9 at 25s; restart at 40s; read the target subject.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the schedule state may not be durable, or the server may re-fire it after restart and duplicate it. The spec gives no detail, so the exact expected behavior is unclear.

promises.quote: If set, the stream will function as a counter stream, hosting distributed counter CRDTs.
promises.plain: The counter value equals the sum of acked increments, even under concurrency and crashes.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill the server during concurrent increments.
promises.outside_observation: After restart, the counter value read from the stream lies between the sum of acked increments and the sum of all attempted increments.
promises.workload_sketch: nats stream add C with AllowMsgCounter; 10 clients publish increment headers to c.x; kill -9; restart; read the last message on c.x.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the running total is computed in memory and may lose acked increments on crash. The spec does not define the counter semantics.

promises.quote: Note, if messages are stored by a stream on a subject that is subsequently removed from the stream config, consumers will still observe those messages if their subject filter overlaps.
promises.plain: Messages on a subject that was later removed from the stream config stay readable, including after a restart.
promises.when_to_inject: Restart the server after removing the subject from the stream config.
promises.outside_observation: A consumer filtered on the old subject still receives every message stored before the change.
promises.workload_sketch: nats stream add S --subjects 'a.>,b.>'; publish to b.x; nats stream edit S --subjects 'a.>'; kill -9; restart; nats consumer add S C --filter 'b.>'; fetch everything.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: recovery may prune messages on subjects that are no longer in the config.

promises.quote: If file-based and a compression algorithm is specified, the stream data will be compressed on disk.
promises.plain: Compressed file storage gives back the exact stored messages after a crash.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill the server during heavy writes to an s2-compressed stream.
promises.outside_observation: Acked messages read back byte-identical after restart. Fuss can also check, read-only, that the block files are not plaintext.
promises.workload_sketch: nats stream add S --compression s2; publish random payloads and record hashes; kill -9; restart; read back and compare hashes.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a block is compressed when sealed, and a crash during compression leaves a block that cannot be decoded.

promises.quote: However, while JetStream does flush file writes to the OS synchronously, under the default configuration it does not immediately `fsync` data to disk.
promises.plain: Messages acknowledged on a file-based stream are already in the OS page cache, so killing only the nats-server process (not the OS) should not lose them.
promises.when_to_inject: SIGKILL nats-server immediately after a burst of publish acks is received, well inside the default 2-minute sync_interval.
promises.outside_observation: After restart, every sequence and Msg-Id that Fuss recorded as acked is returned by `nats stream get` or a full replay. The stream's last sequence is at least the highest acked sequence.
promises.workload_sketch: nats stream add S --subjects s.> --storage file --replicas 1; loop `nats pub s.x <id> --jetstream` while logging each ack's seq; kill -9; restart nats-server with the same -js -sd dir; replay with an ephemeral consumer using deliver all and compare against the log.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: unflushed in-process buffers (for example, write coalescing in the filestore) could hold acked data that was not yet written to the OS when the process died.

promises.quote: For writes (publications to a stream), the formal consistency model of NATS JetStream is [Linearizable](https://jepsen.io/consistency/models/linearizable).
promises.plain: Every acknowledged publish takes effect atomically at a single point between request and ack, consistent with real-time order.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill or restart the stream leader (or random cluster nodes) while concurrent publishers are in flight.
promises.outside_observation: Feed Fuss's log of publish invocations, acks, errors and timeouts, plus the final stream contents, to a linearizability checker. No acked write may be missing. No write may appear ordered before a write that completed before it started. Timed-out writes may appear or not, but at most once.
promises.workload_sketch: Start a 3-node cluster from config files; nats stream add S --replicas 3; N concurrent clients publish unique payloads with timestamps logged; kill -9 the leader mid-run; restart it; read the full stream and check.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a leader change could let a deposed leader ack a write that the new leader never sees.

promises.quote: JetStream uses a NATS optimized RAFT distributed quorum algorithm to distribute the persistence service between NATS servers in a cluster while maintaining immediate consistency (as opposed to [eventual consistency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eventual\_consistency)) even in the face of failures.
promises.plain: In a cluster, stream state stays immediately consistent across failures, with no divergent histories between replicas.
promises.when_to_inject: Rolling kill and restart of nodes, including a minority isolated by stopping and restarting processes, during continuous publishing.
promises.outside_observation: After healing, direct-get requests sent to each replica by sequence return identical messages. Read-only inspection of each node's storage directory shows the same last sequence. No sequence maps to two different payloads across the observation log.
promises.workload_sketch: 3-node cluster; nats stream add S --replicas 3 --allow-direct; continuous publish; repeatedly kill -9 one node and restart it; at the end run `nats stream get S <seq>` against each server and compare.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: catch-up after restart could truncate or skip entries if a snapshot and the log disagree.

promises.quote: Do note, while we do guarantee immediate consistency when it comes to [monotonic writes](https://jepsen.io/consistency/models/monotonic-writes) and [monotonic reads](https://jepsen.io/consistency/models/monotonic-reads).
promises.plain: One client's writes are applied in the order issued, and a client never reads an older state after reading a newer one.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill and restart the leader, or the server the client is connected to, between successive reads or writes from the same client.
promises.outside_observation: Per client, the stream sequences of its sequential publishes strictly increase. Successive reads of the stream's last sequence or last message never go backwards.
promises.workload_sketch: One client publishes p1..pn synchronously and logs seqs; another client repeatedly runs `nats stream info S` or gets the last message by subject, logging the results; kill the leader periodically.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: reads served by a lagging follower or mirror after failover could return an older last-seq.

promises.quote: On the read side (listening to or replaying messages from streams) the formal models don't really apply because JetStream does not support atomic batching of multiple operations together (so the only kind of 'transaction' is the persisting, replicating and voting of a single operation on the stream) but in essence, JetStream is [serializable](https://jepsen.io/consistency/models/serializable) because messages are added to a stream in one global order (which you can control using compare and publish).
promises.plain: All messages get one global order with unique, gap-free sequence numbers, and compare-and-publish (expected last sequence) lets clients control that order.
promises.when_to_inject: Many clients publish with the Nats-Expected-Last-Sequence header at once, with a leader kill mixed in.
promises.outside_observation: Every consumer sees the same order. At most one publisher succeeds for each expected-last-sequence value. Sequence numbers are unique, and the only gaps are explained by deletes.
promises.workload_sketch: Concurrent clients read the last seq, then publish with header Nats-Expected-Last-Sequence=<seq>; log successes and failures; replay the stream from two independent consumers and compare orders.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the expected-sequence check might be evaluated before replication, so two publishers could both pass around a leader change.

promises.quote: In a replicated setup, a published message is acknowledged after it successfully replicated to at least a quorum of servers.
promises.plain: An ack from a replicated stream means a majority holds the message, so losing a minority right after the ack loses nothing.
promises.when_to_inject: kill -9 the stream leader the instant Fuss receives a publish ack.
promises.outside_observation: After a new leader is elected, the acked message is present at its acked sequence.
promises.workload_sketch: 3-node cluster, R3 stream; publish a message, receive the ack, immediately kill -9 the leader; query `nats stream get S <seq>` through the remaining nodes.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the ack might be sent once the leader commits locally, before follower acknowledgements are actually counted.

promises.quote: Replicas=3 - Can tolerate the loss of one server servicing the stream. An ideal balance between risk and performance.
promises.plain: An R3 stream stays available for reads and writes, and loses no acked data, when any one of its servers is down.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill any single replica (leader or follower) and keep it down while the workload continues.
promises.outside_observation: After a brief election, publishes keep getting acks. Earlier acked messages remain readable. No acked message is lost after the node returns.
promises.workload_sketch: 3-node cluster; nats stream add S --replicas 3; continuous publish and consume; kill -9 one node for 60s; restart; verify against the log.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a stuck leader election, or a consumer leader placed on the dead node, could keep the stream unavailable longer than expected.

promises.quote: Replicas=5 - Can tolerate simultaneous loss of two servers servicing the stream. Mitigates risk at the expense of performance.
promises.plain: An R5 stream survives two servers dying at the same moment with no acked data lost and service continuing.
promises.when_to_inject: kill -9 two replicas simultaneously, including the leader, during publishing.
promises.outside_observation: Publishes resume with acks. Every previously acked message is readable from the surviving three nodes.
promises.workload_sketch: 5-node cluster; nats stream add S --replicas 5; publish loop; kill two nodes at once; continue; restart them; verify.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: if the remaining three include a lagging follower, it might win the election and truncate.

promises.quote: Setting a lower `sync_interval` increases the frequency of disk writes, and reduces the window for potential data loss, but at the expense of performance. Additionally, setting `sync_interval: always` will make sure servers `fsync` after every message before it is acknowledged.
promises.plain: With sync_interval: always, every acked message is fsynced to disk before the ack, so even an OS crash cannot lose it.
promises.when_to_inject: Hard power-off or OS crash of the host or VM running nats-server right after acks (requires running nats-server inside a VM Fuss controls).
promises.outside_observation: After the VM reboots and nats-server restarts, every acked message is present in the replay.
promises.workload_sketch: Config with jetstream { sync_interval: always }; nats stream add S --storage file; publish and log acks; hard-reset the VM; restart; replay and compare.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: metadata or index files might not be fsynced together with the message block, so recovery could discard the tail.

promises.quote: The data will be `fsync`-ed no later than this interval.
promises.plain: With the default or a configured sync_interval, data acked longer ago than the interval survives an OS crash.
promises.when_to_inject: Hard reset of the VM more than sync_interval after a batch of acks, with no further writes in between.
promises.outside_observation: Messages acked more than sync_interval before the crash are all present after reboot. Loss is allowed only within the final interval.
promises.workload_sketch: Config sync_interval: 10s; publish batch A, wait 30s, publish batch B; hard-reset the VM within 1s; restart; batch A must be complete.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the sync timer could be skipped or drift under load or wall-clock skew.

promises.quote: When using the JetStream publish calls to publish to streams there is an acknowledgment mechanism between the publisher and the NATS server, and you have the choice of making synchronous or asynchronous (i.e. 'batched') JetStream publish calls.
promises.plain: A publish ack means the message was stored. A publish that fails, for example when the disk is full, must return an error and not be silently acked.
promises.when_to_inject: Fill the filesystem holding the JetStream store directory during a mixed synchronous and asynchronous publish burst, then free the space.
promises.outside_observation: Every acked message is present after space is freed and the server restarts. Every publish that got an error is either absent or appears at most once. No acked message is corrupted or truncated on replay.
promises.workload_sketch: Put the store dir on a small tmpfs or loop device; nats stream add S --storage file; async publish loop logging acks and errors; fill the disk with a dd file; continue; delete the file; restart; replay.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a write error on a message block might be detected only after the ack, or might leave a partial record that breaks recovery of later blocks.

promises.quote: Therefore, JetStream also offers an '_exactly once_' quality of service. For the publishing side, it relies on the publishing application attaching a unique message or publication ID in a message header and on the server keeping track of those IDs for a configurable rolling period of time in order to detect the publisher publishing the same message twice.
promises.plain: Republishing with the same Nats-Msg-Id within the duplicate window stores the message only once, even across crashes and retries.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill the server (or leader) after it receives a publish but before the client gets the ack, then have the client retry with the same Msg-Id after restart.
promises.outside_observation: Each Msg-Id appears exactly once in the stream. Retry acks carry duplicate=true and the original sequence.
promises.workload_sketch: nats stream add S --dupe-window 2m; publish with header Nats-Msg-Id:<uuid>, retrying on timeout with the same id; kill -9 and restart repeatedly; replay and count each id.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the dedup ID table might live only in memory and not be rebuilt from stored messages on restart, so retries after a crash create duplicates.

promises.quote: Therefore, JetStream also offers an '_exactly once_' quality of service. For the publishing side, it relies on the publishing application attaching a unique message or publication ID in a message header and on the server keeping track of those IDs for a configurable rolling period of time in order to detect the publisher publishing the same message twice.
promises.plain: The duplicate window is a rolling time period, so wall-clock jumps should not make the server forget IDs early or block new ones.
promises.when_to_inject: Step the server's clock forward past the dupe window between an original publish and its retry, or backward after a publish.
promises.outside_observation: A retry sent within the real elapsed window is still detected as a duplicate (or Fuss records the deviation). Distinct IDs are never rejected.
promises.workload_sketch: nats stream add S --dupe-window 1m; publish id X; jump the clock +10m with faketime or a namespace clock; republish id X; check whether it is stored twice.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: window expiry is likely computed from wall-clock timestamps, so a forward jump expires IDs immediately.

promises.quote: For the subscribers a _double_ acknowledgment mechanism is used to avoid a message being erroneously re-sent to a subscriber by the server after some kinds of failures.
promises.plain: Once a consumer ack is confirmed by the server (double ack), that message is never redelivered, even after a server crash.
promises.when_to_inject: kill -9 the server right after the client receives the ack confirmation for a message.
promises.outside_observation: After restart, no message whose ack confirmation Fuss logged is ever delivered again on that durable consumer.
promises.workload_sketch: nats consumer add S C --pull --ack explicit; fetch, then AckSync (double ack) and log confirmation; kill -9; restart; keep fetching for longer than ack-wait; check for redeliveries of confirmed seqs.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: consumer ack state may be persisted lazily, so a crash rolls back the ack floor.

promises.quote: * Some consumers support acknowledging _all_ the messages up to the sequence number of the message being acknowledged, some consumers provide the highest quality of service but require acknowledging the reception and processing of each message explicitly as well as the maximum amount of time the server will wait for an acknowledgment for a specific message before re-delivering it (to another process attached to the consumer).
promises.plain: Unacked messages are redelivered after ack-wait, and ack-all acknowledges every earlier message too. This must hold across restarts.
promises.when_to_inject: Restart the server while messages are delivered but unacked, or right after an ack-all.
promises.outside_observation: Every delivered-but-unacked message is eventually redelivered after restart. Nothing below an ack-all sequence is redelivered.
promises.workload_sketch: Two consumers, one --ack explicit and one --ack all, with --wait 5s; fetch 10, ack some (or ack-all on #7); kill -9; restart; fetch again and compare redelivered seqs to the log.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: pending or redelivery state may not survive restart, causing lost messages or redelivery of acked ones.

promises.quote: * Some consumers support acknowledging _all_ the messages up to the sequence number of the message being acknowledged, some consumers provide the highest quality of service but require acknowledging the reception and processing of each message explicitly as well as the maximum amount of time the server will wait for an acknowledgment for a specific message before re-delivering it (to another process attached to the consumer).
promises.plain: The ack-wait timeout governs redelivery timing, so clock jumps should not cause premature mass redelivery or indefinite stalls.
promises.when_to_inject: Jump the server clock forward or backward while messages are pending acks.
promises.outside_observation: Redelivery times measured on Fuss's own monotonic clock stay close to ack-wait. No message is stuck forever after a backward jump.
promises.workload_sketch: Consumer --ack explicit --wait 30s; fetch messages without acking; step the server clock -1h or +1h; record when redeliveries arrive.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: if timers use wall-clock rather than monotonic time, a backward jump could delay redelivery by the size of the jump.

promises.quote:
* You can also send back _negative_ acknowledgements.
* You can even send _in progress_ acknowledgments (to indicate that you are still processing the message in question and need more time before acking or nacking it).
promises.plain: A nak causes prompt redelivery, and an in-progress ack resets the ack-wait timer so the message is not redelivered while work continues.
promises.when_to_inject: Restart the server or consumer leader between a +WPI (in progress) and the final ack, or right after a -NAK.
promises.outside_observation: Naked messages get redelivered. Messages kept alive with in-progress acks are not redelivered to another worker before ack-wait elapses after the last +WPI. Logs show no double processing where none should occur.
promises.workload_sketch: Pull consumer --wait 10s; worker A fetches, sends +WPI every 5s for 30s, then acks; worker B fetches concurrently; inject a restart midway; check whether B ever received A's message.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the in-progress deadline extension may not be persisted or replicated, so after failover the original deadline applies.

promises.quote: * _work queue_ (the stream is used as a shared queue and messages are removed from it as they are consumed) is to provide the exactly-once consumption of messages in the stream.
promises.plain: In a work-queue stream, each message is consumed and removed once, and an acked message never reappears, even after crashes.
promises.when_to_inject: kill -9 the server while several pull workers fetch and ack concurrently.
promises.outside_observation: Across all workers, each message is acked successfully exactly once. After restart, acked messages are absent from the stream (stream info message count and first seq). No message is lost without an ack.
promises.workload_sketch: nats stream add Q --retention work --subjects q.>; nats consumer add Q W --pull --ack explicit; publish 10k unique ids; 4 workers fetch with AckSync; kill -9 and restart repeatedly; tally.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the removal on ack and the consumer ack floor could be persisted at different times, so a crash resurrects consumed messages.

promises.quote: * _interest_ (messages are kept in the stream for as long as there are consumers that haven't delivered the message yet) is a variation of work queue that only retains messages if there is interest (consumers currently defined on the stream) for the message's subject.
promises.plain: In an interest stream, a message stays until every defined consumer has handled it, so no message is dropped before a slow consumer gets it.
promises.when_to_inject: Restart the server after a fast consumer has acked but before a slow consumer has fetched.
promises.outside_observation: After restart, the slow consumer still receives every message. Messages are removed only after all consumers ack.
promises.workload_sketch: nats stream add I --retention interest; consumers FAST and SLOW; publish 1000; FAST acks all; kill -9; restart; SLOW fetches all 1000; stream count drops to 0 afterwards.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: interest checks on restart could run before all consumer states load, causing premature deletion.

promises.quote:
* _discard old_ means that the stream will automatically delete the oldest message in the stream to make room for the new messages.
* _discard new_ means that the new message is discarded (and the JetStream publish call returns an error indicating that a limit was reached).
promises.plain: At a limit, discard-old drops the oldest messages, while discard-new rejects new publishes with an error and never acks them.
promises.when_to_inject: Many concurrent publishers hit max-msgs or max-bytes at once, plus a restart at the limit.
promises.outside_observation: With discard new, the count of acked messages never exceeds the limit, every over-limit publish gets an error, and no errored message appears. With discard old, the stream holds exactly the newest N acked messages.
promises.workload_sketch: nats stream add L --max-msgs 100 --discard new; 10 concurrent publishers send 50 each; count acks vs errors and stream contents; repeat with --discard old and verify the remaining seqs are the newest 100.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a race between concurrent stores might let the limit check pass for several publishes, overshooting.

promises.quote: Note that regardless of the retention policy selected, the limits (and the discard policy) _always_ apply.
promises.plain: Limits are enforced on limits, work-queue and interest streams alike, including after restart.
promises.when_to_inject: Restart the server when a work-queue or interest stream is at its limit.
promises.outside_observation: After restart, the stream never exceeds max-msgs or max-bytes, and discard behavior matches the configuration.
promises.workload_sketch: nats stream add W --retention work --max-msgs 50 --discard new; publish 60 without consuming; check 10 errors; kill -9; restart; publish again and expect an error; count stays at 50.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: limit accounting might be recomputed incorrectly from disk after a crash.

promises.quote: * Maximum message age.
promises.plain: Messages older than max-age are removed, which should behave sanely under clock changes and restarts.
promises.when_to_inject: Step the server clock forward by more than max-age, or backward, while the stream holds messages, and restart.
promises.outside_observation: Fuss records whether messages younger than max-age (by its own clock) vanish after a forward jump, and whether expiry stops after a backward jump. Also checks that expiry still happens after restart.
promises.workload_sketch: nats stream add A --max-age 1m; publish 100; jump the clock +2h; check the stream count; separately publish, kill -9, wait 2m, restart, and confirm the messages expired.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: expiry uses wall-clock message timestamps, so a forward jump instantly purges fresh data.

promises.quote:
* Maximum individual message size.
* You can also set limits on the number of consumers that can be defined for the stream at any given point in time.
promises.plain: Messages over max-msg-size are rejected with an error, and creating consumers beyond max-consumers fails, even under concurrency.
promises.when_to_inject: Many clients create consumers concurrently at the limit, and publish oversize messages.
promises.outside_observation: Successful consumer creations never exceed the limit (`nats consumer ls`). Oversize publishes get errors and never appear in the stream.
promises.workload_sketch: nats stream add C --max-consumers 5 --max-msg-size 1024; 20 parallel `nats consumer add` calls; publish a 2KB payload; verify.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: concurrent consumer creation might check the count before inserting, exceeding the limit.

promises.quote:
* _all_ of the messages currently stored in the stream, meaning a complete 'replay' and you can select the 'replay policy' (i.e. the speed of the replay) to be either:
  * _instant_ (meaning the messages are delivered to the consumer as fast as it can take them).
  * _original_ (meaning the messages are delivered to the consumer at the rate they were published into the stream, which can be very useful for example for staging production traffic).
promises.plain: Deliver-all replays every stored message in order, and replay-original preserves the original inter-message timing.
promises.when_to_inject: Skew the server clock during an original-rate replay, or restart mid-replay.
promises.outside_observation: The replay contains all stored seqs in increasing order. With original replay, inter-arrival gaps on Fuss's monotonic clock match the publish gaps from its log.
promises.workload_sketch: Publish 20 messages 1s apart; create a consumer --deliver all --replay original; measure arrival gaps; jump the clock mid-replay.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: original-rate pacing may compute delays from wall-clock timestamps, so skew causes bursts or long stalls.

promises.quote:
* the _last_ message stored in the stream, or the _last message for each subject_ (as streams can capture more than one subject).
* starting from a specific _sequence number_.
* starting from a specific _start time_.
promises.plain: Consumers can start exactly at the last message, the last message per subject, a given sequence, or a given time.
promises.when_to_inject: Restart the server between publishing and creating or resuming the consumer.
promises.outside_observation: The first delivered message matches the expected seq, per-subject last values, or first message at or after the start time according to Fuss's log.
promises.workload_sketch: Publish to s.a, s.b, s.c multiple times; kill -9 and restart; create consumers with --deliver last-per-subject, --deliver 42, and --deliver <time>; compare first deliveries.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: per-subject index or time index rebuilt after a crash could be stale, giving wrong start points.

promises.quote: Client applications can choose to use fast un-acknowledged `push` (ordered) consumers to receive messages as fast as possible (for the selected replay policy) on a specified delivery subject or to an inbox.
promises.plain: Ordered consumers deliver stream messages in strict sequence order without gaps or duplicates, even across server disruptions.
promises.when_to_inject: Restart or kill the server the ordered consumer is attached to mid-replay.
promises.outside_observation: The sequence of stream seqs received by the client is strictly increasing and contiguous (except for deleted seqs).
promises.workload_sketch: Publish 50k messages; start an ordered consumer (for example `nats sub --stream S` with the ordered option, or the client OrderedConsumer); kill -9 and restart the server midway; check received seqs.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the client-side reset after a server restart may resume from the wrong seq, causing gaps.

promises.quote: Pull consumers can and are meant to be shared between applications (just like queue groups) in order to provide easy and transparent horizontal scalability of the processing or consumption of messages in a stream without having (for example) to worry about having to define partitions or worry about fault-tolerance.
promises.plain: Several clients sharing one pull consumer split the messages between them without loss, and the remaining clients pick up when one dies.
promises.when_to_inject: kill -9 one worker process holding unacked messages, and separately restart the server.
promises.outside_observation: Every message is eventually acked by some worker. Messages held by the dead worker are redelivered to others after ack-wait. Concurrently delivered messages are not given to two workers within ack-wait.
promises.workload_sketch: Pull consumer --ack explicit --wait 5s; 4 worker processes fetch batches of 10; kill one worker; restart the server once; tally acks per message id.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: outstanding pull requests from a dead client may keep absorbing messages until they expire.

promises.quote: JetStream also allows server administrators to easily mirror streams, for example between different JetStream domains in order to offer disaster recovery. You can also define a stream that 'sources' from one or more other streams.
promises.plain: A mirror eventually contains every origin message in the same order, and a sourcing stream gets every source message once, even after restarts.
promises.when_to_inject: Kill and restart the server hosting the mirror or sourcing stream while the origin keeps receiving publishes.
promises.outside_observation: After catch-up, mirror contents equal origin contents seq by seq. Sourced streams contain each origin message exactly once.
promises.workload_sketch: nats stream add O; nats stream add M --mirror O; nats stream add X --source O; publish continuously; kill -9 and restart; compare the streams.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: the source position may be checkpointed lazily, so a restart re-sources messages, creating duplicates in X.

promises.quote: The Key Value store supports atomic `create` and `update` operations. This enables pessimistic locks (by creating a key and holding on to it) and optimistic locks (using CAS - compare and set).
promises.plain: KV create succeeds for only one client when a key is absent, and update succeeds only if the revision matches, under concurrency and crashes.
promises.when_to_inject: Many clients race create or update on the same key, with a leader kill mid-race.
promises.outside_observation: Exactly one create succeeds per key lifetime. Each revision is produced by exactly one successful update. No two clients both believe they hold the lock. Values form a single linear history.
promises.workload_sketch: nats kv add B --replicas 3; 10 clients loop: get key k with revision r, then `nats kv update B k <v> r`; also race `nats kv create B lock`; kill the leader during the run; check the history.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a retry after a timed-out CAS could succeed twice if the expected-revision check is not re-evaluated after failover.

promises.quote: You can subscribe to changes in a Key Value on the bucket or individual key level with `watch` and optionally retrieve a `history` of the values (and deletions) that have happened on a particular key.
promises.plain: Watchers see every change in order, and history lists all retained values and deletes for a key, even across restarts.
promises.when_to_inject: Restart the server while watchers are active and updates continue.
promises.outside_observation: The watch stream's revisions strictly increase, and the final value matches the last successful put. `nats kv history` contains every acked put and delete within the history limit, in order.
promises.workload_sketch: nats kv add B --history 64; watcher on k; writer does puts and deletes, logging revisions; kill -9 and restart; compare watcher output and history to the log.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a watcher reconnecting after restart may skip updates made during the outage.

promises.quote: The key being replaced by a file name and value being designed to store arbitrarily large `objects` (e.g. files, even if they are very large) rather than 'values' that are message-sized (i.e. limited to 1Mb by default). This is achieved by chunking messages.
promises.plain: A large object put either completes and reads back byte-identical, or is not visible as a complete object, even if the server dies mid-upload.
promises.when_to_inject: kill -9 the server partway through a multi-chunk object put.
promises.outside_observation: After restart, `nats object get` either fails or returns bytes whose digest matches the original. A completed put always reads back intact.
promises.workload_sketch: nats object add O; nats object put O bigfile (500MB); kill -9 midway; restart; nats object ls and get; compare sha256.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: chunks may persist without the final metadata message, or the metadata may reference missing chunks after a crash.

promises.quote: * The system must self-heal.
promises.plain: After faults end, the cluster returns to a working, consistent state without manual intervention.
promises.when_to_inject: After a series of kills, restarts and disk-full episodes, stop injecting faults.
promises.outside_observation: Within a bounded time, all streams and consumers report leaders, publishes and fetches succeed, and replicas converge to identical state.
promises.workload_sketch: Run a random fault schedule on a 3-node cluster for 10 minutes; then idle; poll `nats stream info` and `nats consumer info` until healthy, and run a final publish and consume check.
promises.why_it_might_break: Guess: a replica that crashed during disk-full may stay permanently out of sync and need a manual peer-remove.
